Testimony of Adam J. Wickett Hospital Nurse III, Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center In support of funding the 1998 Special Retirement Plan for DDPC & RPC Nurses
My name is Adam Wickett, and I am a Hospital Nurse III at Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center, and I have spent most of my adult life working in inpatient psychiatric nursing for the State of Maine. In 10 years, I will be in my early 50's and I will have worked at DDPC for nearly three decades.
I am proud of my career and of the work we do. I have stayed because I believe in public service, and our patients deserve experienced, committed staff. At the same time, I think it is important to speak honestly about what this job involves, and how it affects people over time.
Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center is a state psychiatric hospital that treats both civil and forensic patients. We do not have a stand-alone forensic unit. IST and NCR patients are integrated across inpatient units, which means nurses throughout the hospital regularly care for court involved patients as part of our normal operations. This is not occasional exposure; it is routine.
Violence is an expected part of inpatient psychiatric nursing. Nurses are present during restraints, assaults, medical emergencies, and behavioral escalations. We work side by side with Mental Health Workers during these events and remain involved throughout, while also carrying responsibility for medical decisions, patient safety, and our professional licenses.
It is also important to describe staffing accurately. We do not have corrections officers on the units. Security support is provided by contract staff whose role is limited and supportive. Clinical decisions and authorization for hands-on interventions rest with licensed nursing staff, who remain present for the duration of incidents. Over years and decades, nurses absorb the physical and psychological effects of this work in a way that does not reset at the end of a shift.
Some nurses sustain injuries that shorten their careers. Others reach retirement without a single catastrophic event but carry lasting effects from repeated exposure to violence and trauma. Even when nurses make it to retirement physically intact, the psychological impact does not disappear.
When Mental Health Worker I-IV positions were added to the 1998 Special Retirement Plan, the State acknowledged the conditions of working in secure inpatient psychiatric settings. Nurses work under those same conditions, during the same incidents, with the same patients. The risks are comparable, and in many cases compounded by additional clinical responsibility. Excluding nurses does not reflect how care is actually delivered in these hospitals.
It is also important to be clear about scope. Not all nursing roles carry the same exposure. Office-based positions and primarily administrative roles do not routinely face the same level of risk. Frontline inpatient nurses, nursing supervisors, and clinical nurse managers do. These staff are placed into staffing counts, respond to codes, cover direct care when staffing falls below minimums, and even sit one-to-one with high-risk patients. Their exposure is part of the job, and cannot be avoided by title.
Page 1 of 2

Testimony of Adam J. Wickett Hospital Nurse III, Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center In support of funding the 1998 Special Retirement Plan for DDPC & RPC Nurses There is also widespread misunderstanding among staff about retirement eligibility. Many nurses believe they must work twenty-five years and reach age fifty-five to retire. Under the 1998 Special Plan, retirement is available after twenty-five years of service or at age fifty-five with 10 years of service. This distinction has a direct impact on retention of frontline workers at both DDPC and RPC. It affects whether experienced staff believe there is a realistic endpoint that does not depend on being injured first. Extending the 1998 Special Retirement Plan to nurses at Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center and Riverview Psychiatric Center would align retirement eligibility with the realities of inpatient psychiatric nurses and support retention of experienced staff in facilities where stability directly affects safety. Thank you for your time and thoughtful consideration.
Respectfully submitted,
Adam J. Wickett BSN, RN Hospital Nurse III Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center This testimony reflects my personal experience and does not represent an official position of my employer.
Page 2 of 2

Adam Wickett Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center LD 2212
I am a Hospital Nurse III at Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center with decades of experience in inpatient psychiatric nursing. This testimony explains why frontline nurses, including supervisor and clinical nurse managers who provide direct patient care, face the same risks already recognized under the 1998 Special Retirement Plan. Extending the plan to nurses at DDPC and RPC would support retention and reflect the realities of inpatient psychiatric care.
197383:
Testimony of Alisha Clavette
My name is Alisha Clavette. I am an RN II at Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center. I have been employed there since March 2, 2009. I am writing to you today to provide testimony on behalf of myself and my coworkers that should help you in making your decision in granting us the
much-needed 25/55 retirement benefit while you work to craft this supplemental budget.
Let me begin by telling you about the clientele that we work with. Many of our patients come to us from jails around the state. A great majority of them have some history of violence. We are
required to work face to face with them for 12-hour shifts, providing support and care that includes treating them with dignity, respect, and compassion. This job is truly not forjust anyone. It is often the case that patients refuse medication and it is a weeks long process to get court ordered medications, leaving these individuals to further decompensate, thus prolonging
their time of stay in the hospital.
My work history at DDPC includes several acts of violence toward me, my coworkers and other patients. My personal experience includes having a patient break my chart room door and arming himself with a 20-inch wooden stake. Another patient holding a pen over my head in a
stabbing manner, and a third patient swinging a metal floor fan by its cord. 3 years ago, I was
punched in the head knocking me off my feet. I have never felt so vulnerable laying on the floor at the feet of a patient who just assaulted me to the point of concussion. I was forced to jump back to my feet as this patient was not even restrained. I missed 2 1/2 shifts after this assault and had to use my own sick time to cover it.
I cannot count the number of times that I have had to intervene by stepping in between patients assaulting other staff or other patients. Our work requires us to physically intervene to maintain safety. Not once have I seen a patient go willingly into a seclusion room or restraint when their level of dangerousness warrants it.
Although over the years our policies surrounding safety have changed greatly, the truth is there
is still a high risk of violence on the units. Too many times I have seen chairs, tables, coffee carafes, hampers and garbage cans being thrown at myself and others. You just can't fix it all.
We instead have to face the reality that the risk is there and the risk is real.
We live in a hyper vigilant state at all times which as you can imagine is not easy and probably
leads to a decreased life expectancy. There are physiological responses during these high stress
interactions that are beyond our control. You see, every time we have to put hands on
somebody, even if only to redirect, our bodies respond with rapid heart rate, increasing blood

pressure, and often a boost of adrenaline. l have seen great nurses become so traumatized after
being assaulted that they could not return to direct patient care. Please ask yourself, could you
return to providing professional quality care to a patient who has assaulted you? That is the reality and the expectation, just return. And act like nothing ever happened.
The state has recently enacted the 25/55 benefit for our mental health workers, they are half of the team. They however depend on the critical thinking skills, rapid assessments and response, and sound clinical judgement skills of us registered nurses.
In closing, budget constraints have always topped the list for reason not to fund these types of "perks." I would like to make you aware that healthcare jobs any place else have a 36-hour fulltime work week. The state of Maine holds us accountable to 40 hours, nurses are working one
36 hour week, and one 44 hour week to average the 40 hours in a two week pay period. We do
not get paid overtime for the hours after 40. Also, we often work 12-hour shifts on holidays, the state only pays for 8 hours. So as you can see it is high time that the state provides us some benefits to help attract new staff and maintain the ones we've got. Thank you for your time and
consideration on this matter.
In Solidarity, Alisha Clavette

Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, members of the Appropriations Committee, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Health and Human Services Committee,
My name is Amy Chery. I am here on my own personal time to speak in support of funding LD 579, An Act to Include Certain Mental Health Workers Under the 1998 Special Plan for Retirement, as part of the Governor's proposed supplemental budget, LD 2212.
In the last budget, many of my coworkers and I were wrongfully excluded from the amended version of LD 579. I am asking this body to correct that exclusion and include the mental health workers who were cut from the bill.
I am a registered nurse and nurse manager at Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center. I have dedicated more than 20 years to caring for individuals with chronic and severe mental illness. I began at the bedside and worked my way into leadership, but I have never stepped away from direct patient care. I continue to respond to emergencies, assist with restraints, intervene in violent incidents, and stand beside my staff when situations escalate.
Mental health nursing has always been my passion. I firmly believe that people with mental illness deserve treatment, dignity, and compassion--not incarceration. Throughout my career, I have taken pride in helping ensure individuals receive care instead of ending up in jail. Those moments when a patient makes progress or regains trust are what keep us committed to this work.
However, the reality has changed. DDPC is increasingly receiving patients directly from jail settings. In correctional facilities, officers can carry weapons, rely on locked cells, and use custody-based safeguards to maintain control. When those same patients arrive at DDPC, those protections are not available. Nurses and mental health workers are expected to manage the same level of aggression and volatility without weapons, without the security infrastructure of a jail, and without the protections correctional staff have. When violence occurs, it is our bodies that absorb it.
I am also a military veteran with 15 years of service, including two deployments to a war zone. I never imagined I would compare my civilian nursing career to my military service, but there are days when the hypervigilance and constant awareness of threat feel painfully familiar. We walk onto the unit knowing violence is not simply possible--it is likely.

I have been verbally, emotionally, and physically assaulted while doing my job. I have been threatened repeatedly, and so have my coworkers. I have had my clothes ripped, my hair pulled, and I have sustained back and shoulder injuries while restraining patients to prevent harm to others. I have witnessed staff members punched, kicked, and choked. These incidents are not isolated--they are part of the daily risk we accept to keep patients and the public safe.
The impact of this work does not end when our shift does. The trauma follows us home. It affects our sleep, our physical health, our emotional well-being, and our families. The cumulative toll of decades in this environment is real. Many of us carry chronic pain, anxiety, and stress that does not simply disappear.
And yet, we continue to show up. We show up because our patients need us. We show up because our coworkers depend on each other for safety. We show up because we believe in the mission of Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center and in protecting our communities. But commitment should not require sacrificing our long-term health and future security.
The 1998 Special Plan is not a privilege--it is recognition of the physical danger, repeated trauma, and emotional strain endured by mental health workers over decades of service. It allows experienced professionals to retire with dignity after years of highrisk work and creates opportunities for new professionals to step into these roles.
LD 579 is about fairness and acknowledging the reality of the work we do every day. If Maine depends on mental health workers to stand unarmed between violence and the public, then Maine has a responsibility to ensure we are not left broken, discarded, or forgotten.
I respectfully ask you to use this surplus to fund LD 579 in the supplemental budget and include the workers who were previously excluded.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Amy Chery, RN

,.
Maine Health Care Association

Testimony of Angela Cole Westhoff, President and CEO Maine Health Care Association
Committee On Appropriations and Financial Affairs
Neither For Nor Against
LD 2212, An Act Making Unified Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations for the
Expenditures of State Government, General Fund and Other Funds, and Changing Certain
Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the
Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027
Tuesday, February 17*" at 1:00 PM

Good afternoon, Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and distinguished members of the Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs; Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer
and distinguished member of the Health and Human Services Committee, I am Angela Westhoff,
President and CEO of the Maine Health Care Association (MHCA).
The MHCA represents more than 200 nursing homes and assisted living/residential care facilities
across Maine. Our mission is to empower our members to ensure the integrity, quality, and
sustainability of long term care in Maine.

I am testifying neither for nor against LD 2212, not for what the Supplemental Budget includes,

but rather for what it fails to address.

_

The Supplemental budget doesn't address COLA for direct care stafl, and it doesn't address the
needed changes to reimbursement rates for nursing facilities.

Regarding COLA: 35 out of 77 nursing homes did not receive the 1% COLA that the legislature approved and appropriated funding for in the last budget. COLA is about ensuring essential direct care
employees are recognized for their value, and that their wages reflect the changing nature of life in America----~the cost of transportation, housing, childcare, etc. In addition, there are no cost of
living adjustments in the supplemental budget to address ongoing increases in the cost of
'
providing care.

1

Regarding the inadequate MaineCare reimbursement rates: The current MaineCare reimbursement rates do not fully cover the cost of care. Without regular rate adjustments, rates remain flat while the cost of providing care continues to rise. The historic direct care worker crisis is a direct reflection of reimbursement rates lagging. Unfortunately, we have a lot of experience with this in the nursing home sector where MaineCare reimbursement
remains flat, the cost of care escalates, and the gap between the two widens. Since 2014, there have been over 50 closures or conversions of long term care facilities in our state. Maine has lost
29 nursing homes and more than 40% of its bed capacity over the last decade. Further, Maine has
the fewest beds per capita of any state in the Northeast. As the oldest state in the nation, with a
significant population of older adults aging and quickly needing our services, this is a deeply
troubling trend.
The exclusion of COLA and the exclusion of improvements to MaineCare reimbursement rates
should be deeply concerning to everyone who cares about Maine's most vulnerable living in nursing and assisted living facilities. You can help prevent additional closures by making sure
that a full COLA is added.
For background, I'll remind the committee that the transition to the new nursing home rate model was implemented on January l, 2025, during which, thanks to the legislature, the Nursing Facility Transition Fund was established as part of PL 2024, Chapter 643. The transition fund was expressly intended to support workforce and retention during the transition to help stabilize the sector, and to support the new rate model.
I note this because there is legislation in this session (LD 213] Resolve, Directing the
Department ofHealth and Human Services to Amend Specific Portions ofthe Nursing Facility Principles ofReimbursement and to Timely Release Quality Payments) which among several
other course corrections would direct DHHS to adjust their order of operations in calculating rates to make COLA not subject to guardrails, retroactive to 1/1/26 so all nursing homes can get
the 1% increase for 2026 and any future COLAs as well. When the transition period is over,
there will be no guardrails and nursing homes will receive COLA without an artificial barrier.
The funding for this fix has already been appropriated, and making this change would be in keeping with the legislative intent in PL 2025, Chapter 388, Part GGG. _
This same bill (LD 2131) would also provide for a partial reinstatement of the direct care add-on at $6.00 per day. This is an important incremental step down approach that could be funded in part by funding existing in the Nursing Facility Transition Fund, and in part with a General Fund
appropriation. It would be a one-time appropriation for the SFY 2026 and this small investment would go a long way to helping with recruitment and retention of caregivers. Long term care facilities have raised caregiver wages by more than 30% over the last few years,
provided sign on bonuses, shift differential pay, and other incentives to help with caregiver
2

wages and benefits. We are making progress on decreasing reliance on temporary nurse agency
labor (also known as contract labor) but after just one year we will see that progress slide
backwards if remove the entire direct care add-on.
In summary, the long-term caregivers need your help. The long term care residents need your help, too. You have the opportunity to help both today, by including adjustments to MaineCare
reimbursement rates and COLA to the Supplemental.
Thank you and I would be happy to answer any questions.

Testimony of Ann~Marie Mayberry
ln Support of LD 2212, Section Z363 and Part G-1
Dear Senator Rotundo and lngwersen, Representatives Gattine and Meyer, and
esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Sen/ices,
My name is Ann-Marie Mayberry. l am from Cape Elizabeth, the CEO of 3Rivers, the
parent of a son diagnosed with Asperger's at age eight, and a long-standing member of the Maine Developmental Services Oversight and Advisory Board, or MDSOAB. I am here today in strong support of LD 2212, Section Z363, and Part G-1.
The MDSOAB is a 15~member, statutorily created board whose sole responsibility is to
provide independent oversight of programs and sen/ices for adults with intellectual
disabilities and autism, primarily those administered by DHHS. Our charge is to provide advice and systemic recommendations to the Commissioner, the Governor, and the
Legislatureon policies, budgets, and legislation affecting the rights and interests of this
population.
In today's environment, independent oversight is not optional--it is essential. We have
all seen recent, deeply troubling reports of abuse, neglect, and exploitation affecting the
IDD population. These incidents underscore why the Legislature created this board and why our work matters.
However, the MDSOAB cannot fulfill its statutory duties with its current budget of
$137,682. That amount covers only a part-time executive director, a contracted bookkeeper, minimal administrative costs, and modest stipends for self-advocates and
Regional Review Committee members. We are not even able to afford an office. There
is simply no capacity for meaningful oversight.
The $58,715 increase proposed by DAFS will allow for competitive wages and benefits
for a part-time Executive Director and a full-time Program Managermpositions essential to performing the work the statute requires.

Equally important is the requested language change in Part G-1, allowing funds to carry forward year to year. Currently, the Board has no cash-flow flexibility, which severely
limits our ability to operate effectively.
Notably, the Board's contract structure has not changed since 2010. During that same period, the compounded CPI has increased by more than 47%. This request represents
the first meaningful funding adjustment in nearly 30 years.
The MDSOAB has been chronically underfunded for decades. Your support of this
DAFS request will finally allow the Board to .carry out the independent oversight role the
Legislature intended---protecting some of Maine's most vulnerable citizens.
Thank you for your consideration.
Very respectfully, Ann-Marie Mayberry
ammayberry@3-rivers.org

Testimony in Support of Annual Cost-of-Living Adjustments to MaineCare Rates

Before the Joint Committees of Appropriations and Health and Human Services

February 17' 2026
Distinguished Members of the Appropriations and Health and Human Services
Committees:
My name is Bart Beattie. I'm a resident of Harpswell and serve as the Chief Operating Officer for Spurwink Services, one of Maine's premiere behavioral healthcare and human
services not-for-profit organizations. With a workforce of over 1,200 dedicated professionals, Spurwink serves more than 10,000 Maine children, adults, and families each
year. 75% of those services are paid for by MaineCare.

I am here today to call for your support of Maine's behavioral healthcare system through the continuation of
annual cost-of-living adjustments to MaineCare reimbursement rates.

As you know, and as was the case last legislative session, funding for these COLAs has been excluded from the governor's proposed budget. You may also be aware that LD2177 has proposed language that would essentially codify the practice of excluding COLAs. These changes undo a clear legislative mandate that MaineCare reimbursement rates receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment. That mandate was enacted by the legislature to ensure that rates keep pace with the real and unavoidable costs of providing services, particularly labor--driven
services that are the safety net for thousands of Mainers.

The predictable result of not applying cost--of-living adjustments is reimbursement rates that fall below the cost of providing care, forcing providers to limit services, reduce capacity, or stop accepting MaineCare altogether. At a
time when affordable healthcare is under attack by the federal government, further limiting access to care to those who most need it is something that I would imagine we all agree must be avoided.
When MaineCare rates fail to reflect actual costs, access to services is constrained. You need not speculate about
the consequences of constrained access ---- lack of access to required services is precisely what led to the most recent Department oflustice lawsuit and its resulting settlement. Rolling back the COLA mandate moves MaineCare policy in the wrong direction and risks repeating those same failures.
I'd also like to remind you that while almost every industry and business has the ability to adjust prices when costs increase, MaineCare providers do not. My wife owns a small retail business in Brunswick. As the cost of
goods and wages have spiked, she has had to increase her prices to keep her business sustainable. She didn't want to as she cares deeply about her customers, but she knew she had to if she wanted to stay in business. I'm on the local school board. Even the school district has the ability to increase its revenue to match its costs. It requires an increase in property taxes - something no one wants -- but it's the reality of what is needed for schools to continue
to meet the community need. MaineCare providers see the exact same increases in costs. However, we can't
increase our prices. We can't close the revenue gap by appealing directly to taxpayers. We rely and depend on you
to ensure our prices -- the MaineCare rates -- keep pace with inflation. That is why only a few years ago you enacted a law to ensure rates at least keep pace with increased labor costs. That's what these very modest cost-of-
living adjustments are for.

l urge you to appropriate the funding for cost-of-living adjustments to MaineCare rates in order preserve the intent
of the laws you passed, ensure continued access to quality care to those who need it most, and to account for the
reality that MaineCare providers experience increased costs just like every other business and family does.

Thank you for your consideration.

Bart Beattie, LCSW
Chief Operating Officer, Spurwink Services, inc.

including workers at the Department of Health and Human Services, as well as in all three branches of
Maine State Government.
We're here today to testify neither for nor against LD 2212, the Governor's proposed Supplemental Budget, and to make recommendations for a fair supplemental budget that ensures quality public services for all Maine people and provides state workers with the respect they have earned but long been denied.
We support the creation of new positions within the Office of MaineCare Services to increase staffing related to required training and compliance due to the federal H.R.1 bill. We also support the numerous

TESTIMONY SUBMITTED TO: Joint Standing Committees on Appropriation and Financial Affairs & Health and Human Services
PUBLIC HEARING DATE: 02/17/2026
Senator Rotondo, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Gattine, Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services:
My name is Brett Bulmer, and I serve as Executive Director of Independence Association, a nonprofit organization based in Brunswick that supports people with intellectual and developmental disabilities in Midcoast Maine. We provide an array of residential and community supports and employ Direct Support Professionals (DSPs) who deliver hands-on care every day.
I am neither for nor against LD 2212 overall. However, I respectfully urge you to include and fully fund the 3.1% Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA) for Direct Support Professionals in the Supplemental Budget.
Under Maine law (22 M.R.S.A. �3173-J), annual cost-of-living adjustments are required for MaineCare services. For the second year in a row, however, the required COLA has not been fully included in the budget. Since being adopted as part of MaineCare Rate Reform in 2022, COLAs have been essential in helping service rates keep pace with inflation and rising labor costs, including maintaining wages at 125% of minimum wage. In a state facing a significant direct care workforce shortage and an annually increasing minimum wage, a COLA is not a luxury--it is a necessity.
In recent months, there has been increased emphasis on service quality, including the formation of OADS' Quality Improvement Coalition and the recent launch of the State's new Licensing system for providers. I appreciate that focus. But as I approach 29 years in this field--having started as a Direct Support Professional myself in 1997--my conviction has only grown stronger: nothing impacts the quality of life for the individuals we serve more than the quality of the staff supporting them. The quality of our services will never exceed the quality of our DSPs. Investing in them through competitive wages isn't optional, it's essential.
We can strengthen oversight and improve systems, but without a stable, adequately compensated workforce, quality will remain fragile. When wages stagnate, turnover rises. When turnover rises, relationships are disrupted. And when relationships are disrupted, people we support experience the greatest impact.
If the State is going to rely on community-based providers to deliver these essential services, it has an obligation to ensure providers have the resources necessary to recruit and retain a qualified workforce. Funding the statutorily required COLA is a critical part of that responsibility.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I respectfully urge you to fund the required 3.1% COLA in the Supplemental Budget.
Respectfully submitted,
Brett Bulmer, Executive Director

Neither for Nor Against LD 2122, An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027

February 17, 2026
Good afternoon, Senator Rotondo, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Gattine, Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services. Thank you for the opportunity to testify on LD 2122, the Governor's Supplemental Budget, An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027.
My name is Bridget McCabe and I serve as the Manager of Policy and Legislative Affairs at 3Rivers. I am submitting testimony neither for nor against LD 2122, An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027. I write today to urge the Legislature to restore the Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA) for MaineCare direct care services within the supplemental budget.
3Rivers is a statewide nonprofit organization supporting people with disabilities across Maine, with services rooted in the local communities where people live. We support individuals in rural and urban areas, including small towns and larger communities throughout the state. Our staff work alongside people in their homes, workplaces, and neighborhoods, supporting meaningful participation in community life through a range of services. We support approximately 500 individuals across Maine who are supported by 355 direct support and care staff. The decisions made in this supplemental budget will affect not only the hardworking individuals who provide critical support throughout our communities, but also the stability of the systems that serve thousands of older adults, people with physical, intellectual, and developmental disabilities, and individuals with behavioral health needs. Cost-of-living adjustments, the mechanism that allows wages, taxes, and benefits to keep pace with inflation, were established by the 130th Legislature for MaineCare direct care service programs. For the second consecutive year, however, these adjustments have not been fully included in the budget as required under statute. Maine law (22 M.R.S.A. �3173-J) requires an annual cost-of-living adjustment for MaineCare services. These adjustments are not optional enhancements; they are a simple but critical tool to help agencies and direct support professionals keep pace with inflation, rising housing costs, and increasing operational expenses. Since being adopted as part of MaineCare rate reform in 2022, COLAs have helped maintain service rates aligned with wage and labor expectations, including the state's goal of reaching or sustaining wages at 125% of the minimum wage. Maine continues to face a significant direct care workforce shortage, compounded by an annually adjusted minimum wage, which increased this year by 3.07%, from $14.65 to $15.10. In this context, an annual COLA is not a luxury; it is a necessity. These adjustments have helped community-based agencies retain experienced and dedicated staff and stabilize critical services across the state.

We are grateful to members of both committees for restoring a partial COLA in last year's budget. That action demonstrated a shared understanding of the importance of maintaining workforce stability in essential care systems. At 3Rivers, workforce pressures remain significant. Like many providers, we continue to experience open positions, increased onboarding and training costs, and the operational strain that accompanies staffing shortages. When positions remain vacant, services may be delayed, reduced, or placed under significant pressure. COLAs have helped slow turnover and improve retention, allowing us to maintain continuity of care and better support the individuals we serve. Even modest stability in wage growth has a measurable impact on our ability to recruit and retain qualified staff. Predictability is equally important. A reliable COLA schedule would allow providers to plan responsibly for wages, programming, and long-term service capacity. It would support more consistent workforce investments and strengthen our ability to meet community needs. Conversely, uncertainty in rate setting, including pending Home and Community-Based Services rate determinations without a clear effective date, complicates planning and creates real concern about long-term sustainability. Providers have engaged in this process in good faith, and continued uncertainty places strain on organizations striving to maintain service access. Without restoration of a 3.1% COLA in this supplemental budget, the erosion of an already fragile care system will continue. When wages stagnate, the consequences extend beyond the workforce, turnover and understaffing disrupt care and increase strain on people who rely on these supports every day. The stability and consistency offered by a predictable COLA schedule are essential to maintaining access to services for many of Maine's most vulnerable residents. Ensuring appropriate compensation for direct support professionals signals that Maine values both its workforce and the individuals they serve. Restoring COLAs is a practical, statutorily supported step toward maintaining service stability and protecting access to care. I respectfully ask the Legislature to allocate and fund the necessary COLA for direct support professionals providing services to adults and children with intellectual and developmental disabilities, individuals with autism spectrum disorder, and people with brain injuries. Thank you for your time and consideration. Respectfully submitted, Bridget McCabe Manager of Policy and Legislative Affairs 3Rivers bmccabe@3-Rivers.org

Christine Vincent Opportunity Enterprises LD 2212
Dear Chairs and Members of the HHS and Appropriations Committees, The Maine State Legislature is about to make decisions on the Supplemental Budget that affect not only the hardworking individuals who provide critical support to our communities, but also the very fabric of compassion and care that sustains us all. At issue is the restoration of the MaineCare Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA) for Direct Care Services. Cost-of-living adjustments -- the mechanism by which wages, taxes, and benefits are able to keep pace with inflation -- were established by the 130th Legislature as part of MaineCare Rate Reform. They are required under Maine law (22 M.R.S.A. �3173-J). Yet for the second year in a row, they have not been included in the budget as required. These programs serve thousands of older adults, people with physical disabilities, people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, individuals with brain injuries, and individuals with behavioral health needs. The stability of these services depends directly on the stability of the workforce. Why This Matters 1. COLAs are required under Maine law. Annual cost-of-living adjustments for MaineCare services are required under 22 M.R.S.A. �3173-J. The Legislature created a predictable, transparent system in 2022 to ensure rates kept pace with economic realities. Failing to fund the COLA undermines that statutory framework. 2. In a minimum-wage state, COLAs are not optional. Maine's minimum wage increases annually. This year alone it rose 3.07%, from $14.65 to $15.10. MaineCare service rates were structured to support wages at or near 125% of minimum wage. COLAs are the mechanism that keeps those wage floors intact. Without them, providers are immediately underwater. In a state facing a direct care workforce shortage, an annual COLA is not a luxury -- it is a necessity. 3. COLAs have worked. Since being introduced in 2022 and fully funded in FY23 and FY24, COLAs have been instrumental in helping community-based agencies retain dedicated staff and stabilize services statewide. They helped agencies: �Increase wages, �Reduce turnover, �Prevent service closures, and �Maintain access for vulnerable Mainers. They have been a lifeline. 4. Without restoration, erosion continues. Last year, thanks to advocacy from providers, workers, people receiving services, and families, lawmakers restored a partial COLA in the budget. That action prevented even deeper destabilization. Without restoration of the 3.1% COLA in this Supplemental Budget, continued erosion of an already fragile system will accelerate. Providers cannot absorb inflation, mandated wage increases, rising housing costs, insurance premiums, utilities, food, transportation, and growing regulatory compliance expenses without corresponding rate adjustments. 5. Workforce stability equals service stability. When wages remain stagnant, it is not just workers who suffer -- it is the people they support. High turnover and understaffing create: �Disruptions in care, �Increased emergency placements, �Greater reliance on institutional settings, �And higher long-term costs to the state. By ensuring that direct support professionals and other direct care workers are

compensated appropriately, the Legislature sends a clear message: we value this workforce and the people who rely on them every day. The Bottom Line The COLA is not new spending. It is not an enhancement. It is the statutory mechanism designed to prevent erosion of service capacity in a minimum-wage, inflation-driven economy. Restoring the 3.1% COLA in the Supplemental Budget is essential to: �Honor Maine law, �Preserve workforce stability, �Prevent service closures, and �Protect thousands of vulnerable Mainers who depend on community-based care. I respectfully urge the HHS and Appropriations Committees to restore the COLA and uphold the rate reform framework that was designed to bring predictability and stability to MaineCare services. Thank you for your leadership and your commitment to Maine's most vulnerable citizens. Respectfully, Christine Vincent

Neither for Nor Against LD 2122, An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027
February 17, 2026 Good afternoon, Senator Rotondo, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Gattine, Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services Thank you for the opportunity to testify on LD 2122, the Governor's Supplemental Budget, An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027.
My name is Christopher Allen, and I'm a Direct Support Professional and Employment Specialist in Island Falls, Maine. I've been a DSP for 12 years, and I'm here today to ask you to restore funding for needed costof-living adjustments in the supplemental budget. I love this work. Supporting people in the northern part of the state so they can live full lives, be part of their communities, and feel valued has been incredibly rewarding. When wages are competitive, DSPs can stay in these roles long enough to build real relationships and provide consistent, quality support. But this job has also become harder every year. The cost of living keeps going up, and while past COLAs helped us stay afloat, they haven't kept pace. High turnover, short staffing, and burnout are now constant challenges. DSPs are expected to do physically, emotionally, and mentally demanding work -- often for wages that are lower than what fast food or convenience stores offer, with far less responsibility. That reality pushes people away from this field, even when they want to do this kind of work. When staff leave, it's not just workers who are affected -- it's the people who rely on us every day for stability, safety, and support. COLAs aren't a bonus or a luxury. They're what allow agencies to stay staffed and services to keep running. They are the backbone of direct care services, not just here in Maine, but across the country. I want to thank members of both committees for restoring a partial COLA in last year's budget. That support mattered, and I'm asking you to continue building on it so this essential workforce can survive and continue serving our communities. Thank you for your time and for listening. Respectfully Submitted,
Christopher Allen CLAllen@3-Rivers.org

Senator lngwerson, Representative Meyer, Senator Grohoski, Representative Gattine,
and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and
Financial Affairs and Health and Human Sen/ices: my name is Courtney Shank and l live in Gorham, ME. l am here today to testify neither for nor against LD 2212.
l am here as someone directly impacted by the proposed federal health care cuts. l am
a full-time college student, working a part-time job that does not provide health
insurance benefits. I do not receive financial support from my parents. MaineCare is the only reason I am able to access health care while working to build a stable future for
myself.
Without MaineCare, I would not be able to afford doctor's visits, prescriptions, or mental
health care. As a student balancing classes, work, and basic living expenses like car
insurance and tuition, there is simply no room in my budget for private insurance premiums or unexpected medical bills. Losing coverage would mean delaying care, going without medications, or facing debt that could follow me for years.
According to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, these federal cuts would reduce funding to health care providers across Maine. That means fewer services, longer wait times, potential job losses, and even hospital closures -- especially in rural areas. When providers lose funding, patients lose access. Students,
working families, seniors, and people with disabilities will all feel the impact.
At the same time, national analysis from the Center for American Progress shows that
these Medicaid cuts are being used to help finance massive tax cuts for corporations and the wealthiest Americans. That includes the wealthiest Mainers. It is hard to
understand why students and working people should lose health care so that those at
the top can receive more tax breaks.
I am doing even/thing I am supposed to do -- working, studying, and trying to become
- self-sufficient. MaineCare is not a handout; it is a bridge that allows me to stay healthy
while l invest in my education and future career. Cutting it would not encourage work
it would make it harder to succeed.
lf the federal government chooses to reduce its commitment to Medicaid, Maine must
step up. We need to raise progressive revenue from corporations and ultra-wealthy
Mainers to backfill these cuts, fully fund MaineCare, and continue expanding access to
care. Health care should not disappear for students like me because of decisions made
in Washington.

Health care is a human right; no one should be sick because they are poor and no one
should be poor because they are sick. I urge you to protect MaineCare and ensure that students, workers, and vulnerable Mainers do not lose the coverage that keeps us healthy and able to contribute to our communities.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Testimony in favor of the Governors Supplemental Budget for the Maine Developmental Services Oversight and Advisory Board- section Z363
Dear Senator Rotundo, Senator lngwersen, Representative Gattine, Representative Myer
and Esteemed Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
and Appropriations and Financial Affairs:
My name is Cullen Ryan, and I serve as the Chair of the Maine Developmental Services
Oversight and Advisory Board (OAB). I have served in this role since 2014 and have served
on the OAB since its inception in 2010. I am also a parent of a 29-year-old man with
intellectual/developmental disabilities. He still lives at home with me, largely because of a
lack of options for independent living that might suit him, given his lack of skills and
capabilities.
The OAB was established as a mechanism of compliance under 34-B for the Consent
Decree to ensure adults with intellectual/developmental disabilities are served adequately,
with input and guidance from a cross-section of people in the system. The OAB strategically includes people who are recipients of services, parents, service providers, and advocates who have spent their entire careers working within the system and have a
fundamental understanding of the sector. This Board provides oversight, guidance, and
insights to DHHS to help optimize the system. it reviews data, analyzes shortcomings, and
assists with systemic improvements.
Fifteen Board members serve voluntarily on the OAB. These are very dedicated people with an enormous amount of collective experience and wisdom. The entire organization is currently held together by one staff member, the Board's Executive Director. The budget has remained unchanged for all 16 years of the Board's existence. As you know, costs have increased since 2010, and the budget doesn't reach as far as it used to. it never was adequate to meet the needs of the organization, and volunteers have been caretaking this. Our past two executive directors have stepped up to help well after their retirement, but each can only last so long in this role. The current ED is in her 80's and has wrestled with
serious medical challenges while admirably fulfillingthe role as best she can. We have run
out of heroes. The OAB has been unable to attract the talent it needs to properly staff the
organization and provide this statutorily required service to the population.
The supplemental budget before you offers a long-sought remedy. The modest increase in the OAB's operating budget would allow the organization to attract and retain staff to work
to fulfill requirements under the statue. This will allow DHHS and the 6000 people served to much more fully benefit from the assembly of talented volunteers serving on the Board.

This is a miniscule part of the Supplemental Budget. But it will much better allow the intention of this statute to be met, something many dedicated people have worked for over
the past decade and a half.
The insights offered by this Board are invaluable. They allow DHHS to optimize its strategies, which is the best possible way to maximize efficiency. When we get the system right, when we properly serve each person, we eliminate costly crises, inefficiencies, and
better allow everyone to be included in society. Given the magnitude of Maine's investment in this sector, proper guidance and oversight is a very small and key investment
that is wise.
Our system is imperfect. Of note, the last Quarterly Report reflected 11,498 Reportable Events in 3 months - a good reason for an oversight body. And, as of the last Quarterly Report from OADS, there are 2,332 people just on the Section 21 services waitlist.
The statute called for Maine to put proper safeguards in place. Faith in that commitment
allowed the Consent Decree to be closed. We are currently neglecting that commitment.
Please include the portion of the budget that will more properly fund the OAB for the first time in 16 years so we can follow the law and make right by that commitment. People like my son and 6000 others deserve nothing less.

Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, members of the joint standing committee on

Appropriations and Financial Affairs and the joint standing committee on Health and Human

Services. My name is Danielle Charles and I represent AllMed Staffing Of New England and our

amazing caregivers. I want to explain why cost-of-living adjustments, or COLAs, are essential

for home care agencies serving MaineCare clients. Unlike private-pay services,

MaineCare-funded programs cap what agencies can charge for each visit. That means when

the cost of doing business goes up wages, insurance, training, transportation, and everything

else our reimbursement does not. Without COLAs, we simply do not have the funding to raise

caregiver wages, even when the cost of living continues to rise. And this has real

consequences.

Personal Support Specialists and direct care workers do some of the most demanding

and meaningful work in our communities. They care for older adults and people with disabilities

who rely on them every day. But when wages cannot keep up with basic living costs, caregiving

becomes less about answering a calling and more about whether someone can afford to stay in

the job.

Many caregivers working in MaineCare-funded services must rely on public assistance

themselves for health insurance, food, and other basic needs simply to survive. These are

hardworking professionals providing essential care, yet reimbursement limits effectively keep

their wages so low that they remain dependent on the very support systems their work helps

sustain. Without COLAs, the system creates a cycle. Agencies cannot raise pay. Workers

cannot achieve financial stability. And more people must rely on public assistance.

But if reimbursement allowed wages to rise meaningfully, many caregivers could move toward

independence and eventually off subsidies. Supporting the workforce is not just an expense it is

a long-term investment in economic stability and reduced reliance on public programs.

COLAs are not a luxury. They are necessary to sustain the workforce, stabilize agencies,

and ensure people receive the care they depend on.

I urge you to ensure that cost-of-living adjustments are added into the budget as intended by the

current rate setting system. Thank you for your consideration of my testimony.

Danielle Charles

AllMed Staffing Of New England

Augusta/Windham

David Cowing Woolwich LD 2212
Dear Senator Rotondo, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Gattine, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services,
I am taking this opportunity to write to you in support of LD 2122, the Governor's Supplemental Budget, An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027.
My name is David Cowing and I live in Woolwich. I am also a member of the MDSOAB. My son has an intellectual disability as well as other disabilities, including significant mental health challenges. He lives in a group home in Bath. Though a current family medical emergency prevents me from attending the hearing on LD 2122, I wanted to be sure to send this brief note because of how strongly I, and the rest of my family, feel about its careful consideration.
Fully funding COLAs for Direct Support Workers has a direct bearing on my son's quality of life at his group home as well as with his participation in the local community. His mental health is significantly affected by not knowing who will be working at his home, something that frequently happens and creates real problems for him. Successful community access is highly dependent on skilled staff, and problems arise when staff who do not know him well are asked to provide the support he requires. I believe there is a direct relationship between consistency of skilled staffing at his home and providing a living wage to the Direct Support Professionals who support him. I ask that you support fully funding COLAs for DSPs in the supplemental budget.
Also, as a father and member of the MDSOAB, I am acutely aware of the important role the MDSOAB can play in ensuring Mainers with developmental disabilities are able to access quality community-based services. As the only statutorily named entity responsible for oversight, it is impossible to fulfill this important role with the very limited staff time currently available. Independent oversight of our support system is a necessity given the growing number of providers and people living in smaller homes, often without skilled supervision. We need to recognize that Mainers like my son with IDD and mental health challenges are among the most vulnerable of our citizens. Providing the MDSOAB with the resources it needs to fulfill its mission is critical.
I want to thank members of both committees for restoring a partial COLA in last year's budget, as well as for the support you've shown in the past for Mainers with IDD and autism. I ask that you continue to demonstrate your support for providing quality services to Mainers with disabilities by supporting LD 2122.
Thank you,
David Cowing Woolwich
10060516:
Testimony of Debbie Dionne Parent and Guardian
Founding Board member of Community Connect Maine Board Member of Independence Association
Neither for Nor Against
LD 2122, An Act of Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government show the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027
Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs & Health and Human Services February 17, 2026
My name is Debbie Dionne and I live in Topsham. After retiring in 2009 from a 35-year career as a teacher at Brunswick Junior High School, I became a full time, volunteer, disability advocate.
Since then, I have submitted testimony every legislative session urging this body to ensure that direct care workers are paid wages that truly reflect the depth of their professional responsibilities. These professionals provide complex, hands-on care to children and adults with disabilities and to our elderly citizens. They administer medications, manage medical and behavioral needs, assist with all activities of daily living, and quite literally safeguard lives. The level of skill, accountability, and emotional investment required of them is significant.
Some years we have made progress. Many years we have not. The reality remains: direct care workers in Maine are still grossly underpaid. Too many must work multiple jobs or excessive overtime just to support their own families. That is not sustainable for them, and it is not safe for the vulnerable people who depend on a stable, well-supported workforce. Meanwhile, Maine continues to face a severe health care workforce crisis, with alarming vacancy rates and more than 100 residential homes closed due to staffing shortages directly tied to insufficient reimbursement rates.
I am also the mother and guardian of Kate, a 46-year-old woman with cerebral palsy, an intellectual disability, and a seizure disorder. My husband and I are now facing life-changing medical challenges of our own, which have significantly increased my responsibilities at home and as a caregiver.
Thankfully, Kate has lived in a Waiver 21 group home for the past 24 years. She depends on the Direct Support Professionals in her home to support her most personal and complex needs 24 hours a day. Kate and her five housemates thrive on consistency and the deep trust they build with their staff. When a DSP leaves, it is not simply a staffing change -- it is a devastating loss.
Each departure means trust must be rebuilt and communication reestablished. For my daughter and many others like her, this disruption can quickly become a crisis. Kate is nonverbal and communicates in alternative ways. When she is not understood, the consequences can be

serious -- refusal to eat or drink, withdrawal, self-injury, behavioral outbursts, or signs of acute depression. These are not "behavior problems." They are expressions of fear, confusion, and loss that Kate has unfortunately experienced.
We must retain the highly trained, experienced, compassionate DSPs who choose to do this demanding work.
Since the COLA was established in 2022 and fully funded in FY23 and FY24, it has been a critical lifeline in stabilizing services across Maine. Because of persistent advocacy from providers, workers, people receiving services, and family members like me, lawmakers acted last year to restore partial COLA funding in the budget. For that, I am sincerely grateful.
But a Cost-of-Living Adjustment written into statute should not be optional. When it is omitted from the supplemental budget for two consecutive years, it undermines the very stability it was designed to protect.
These workers are not asking for something new. They are asking for what was already promised.
If we truly value people with disabilities and the elderly in our state, then we must value the workforce that makes their safety, dignity, and independence possible. Funding the statutory COLA is not just a budget decision. It is a statement about our priorities. It is fiscal integrity. And it is a moral obligation.
For Kate. For the thousands of vulnerable Mainers like her. And for the professionals who quietly hold their lives together every single day -- I urge you to fully fund the statutory COLA.
Thank you for your consideration.
Respectfully Submitted,
Debbie Dionne' Topsham, Maine

Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, members of the Appropriations Committee, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, members of Health and Human Services Committee, I'm Deirdra Raymond. I am here on my own personal time to speak in support of funding LD 579 as part of the Governor's proposed Supplemental Budget known as LD 2212.
I have been working in psychiatry as a direct care Registered nurse since 1996. I would not benefit from 25/55 because being a single parent, I needed the flexibility of working per diem and contract until my daughter turned 18 this year due to chronic issues she was dealing with. I was full time but with flexibility. So, I don't have much to gain except to put forth what I truly believe in. It seems that nurses working in psych were not included in the amended version of LD 579 biennial budget (only Mental Health workers, which is a different specialty from nurses although just as crucial), which is absolutely shocking. The original bill included nurses that work in psych, and my coworkers and I are asking for you to fix this problem in LD 2212.
The bill as written post amendment only includes the Mental Health Worker **role** which specifically refers to entry level or CNA licensed orderlies, which excludes all other direct care staff at DDPC and Riverview, including Nurses, outpatient crisis workers, social workers, and many others who are also subject to the high levels of stress and physical risk inherent to the mental health care field. It's clear based on the testimony provided in support of LD 579 prior to the bill being amended on June 11th that the intention of the bill was not to exclude these roles. Also, the Mental Health Worker role, due to its nature as an entry level role in addition to the high stress level of the work, has a very high turnover rate, and many Mental Health Workers end up using the role as a steppingstone into becoming nurses, and thus lose eligibility for 25/55. This can be clearly seen by the fact that the budgetary estimate for DHHS 25/55 retirement post amendment was just under $60,000, while the previous estimate less estimates from the other sections would have amounted to over $5,000,000.
We are on the front lines going out on the floor managing violent, assaultive psychiatric patients trying to keep them, their peers and our peers safe. We have been hit, kicked, spit on, slapped, pushed, accused, called names and insulted mercilessly at times daily during our careers. We have no weapons, just an understanding of how to deal with these situations due to training and experience. We come to work with the knowledge that we may not come out the same way we went in. It is a job that can be thankless and cruel. The level of stress many of us carry does affect our own mental health but because we believe in what we do, we come back every scheduled day.
Please consider 25/55 for nurses working in these positions as well. Nurses who work in these roles provide an absolutely essential and irreplaceable service to our community and deserve to

be rewarded for their time served in such a physically, psychologically, and emotionally demanding field. Sincerely, Deirdra Raymond RN,BSN

LeadingAge Maine & New Hampshire is an association representing mission-driven senior living and long-term care providers in Maine and New Hampshire. Our member organizations include nursing homes, assisted living programs, federally-assisted and market-rate housing, and Life Plan Communities (continuing care retirement communities). Our Mission: Inspiring our members to pursue innovation and the best life for older adults. Our Vision: LeadingAge Maine & New Hampshire is a recognized, transformational leader in shaping society's vision of aging.
Testimony of Denise M Vachon, Government Affairs, LeadingAge Maine and New Hampshire Submitted to
The Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee and The Health and Human Services Committee with regard to
LD 2212 An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the FYs ending June 30, 2026 and June 30,
2027
February 17, 2026
Senators Rotundo and Ingwersen, Representatives Gattine and Meyer, and Members of the Appropriations and Financial Services and Health and Human Services Committees
My name is Denise Vachon, I live in Farmingdale, and I speak today on behalf of MaineCare-participating nursing care and assisted living members of LeadingAge Maine & New Hampshire. Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony neither for nor against LD 2122.
We recognize that this budget cycle is extremely weighty, and its very crafting is being made within challenging fiscal constraints and in response to significant changes in federal funding. We appreciate your thought leadership regarding the cost and commitments of the MaineCare system from various perspectives, and recognize your dedication to serving the citizens of Maine. Finally, we recognize that this budget is carefully considered in the context many other first priorities.
With that, on behalf of its providers, the care teams, and especially the residents and their families that we serve, let me begin, on behalf of LeadingAge ME NH and its members, by thanking you for your tireless work.
TESTIMONY As we contemplate the Supplemental budget, we are grateful for DHHS' commitment to continued funding for direct care workers at 125% of minimum wage. We believe that that consideration is "baked into" this budget.
In support of your work, I offer the observation that there are several important bills having been heard but not yet worked by the HHS Committee that could have budgetary impacts to the long-term care and aging services sector. We will appreciate your "holding room" for funding that might result from these bills.
� LD 1932 An Act to Support Essential Support Workers and Enhance Workforce Development attempts to rectify the shortfall in COLAs as a result of the last Supplemental Budget. We continue to be deeply grateful for the efforts for remedy by the HHS Committee in the first session. However, that shortfall, coupled with the apparent lack of funding for a COLA in this Supplemental is concerning. We urge your consideration of and commitment to fully funding of COLAs in the Supplemental Budget as well as to include consideration for innovations, technology and data collection.
� LD 2177 An Act to Update and Improve the MaineCare Reimbursement System

is intended to modify the MaineCare rate-setting system. A key concern is the signal of unreliability of reimbursement for providers, as represented by language that makes funding "subject to [appropriations]". The suggestion that the prioritization of funding may diminish for the services and supports that the citizens of Maine rely on to be there when they need them is most worrisome. It suggests an erosion of the mutual commitments made between the State and the Providers, where the State commits to reimbursement of reasonable approved costs, in exchange for the Providers' commitment to make MaineCare supported services and supports available, with excellence in personcentered practices.
� LD 2131 An Act to Preserve and Improve Access to Nursing Facility Services in the State is specific to Nursing Care providers, and calls for the payments and adjustments related to rate reform - already approved - to be released: specifically the release of quality bonus payments, promised in December, 2025; relief to certain providers caught unintentionally by the "calculation of guardrails", and the partial reinstatements of direct care add-on payments.
We ask that note be made that the resolution of these bills may come with fiscal notes and related consideration in the budget.
Having led a provider community for nearly my entire career, I cannot over-state my view that the MaineCare system is a delicate nexus of services and supports where the sustainability of one service line or sector relies on the sustainability of all others. And, the success and sustainability of each service line and sector relies on a qualified, well-trained, committed staff members who are fairly and competitively compensated to assure consistent qualified and heartful care for those we serve - the citizens of Maine.
Speaking for the sector I represent: When funding for Nursing Facilities and Assisted Living Facilities is reliable, providers are more stable, can invest in their staff and residents, and the citizens of our state worry less about closures, and access to care in their home communities. Families can remain in the workforce without worry about their loved one's care and safety, rather than give up their livelihood to care for their person. The State economy is well-served. The need for public supports for those who could otherwise be gainfully employed is lessened.
When the long-term care sector is properly funded and functioning, it eases the burden on hospitals, relieving the strain of inappropriately placed individuals there, so that others with acute needs have access. In turn, that same funding serves to keep MaineCare resources fully activated (beds remain open, staffing is addressed). In turn again, fully activated resources provide access to those on wait lists. And, since those on wait lists can be more readily served, the burden on and wait lists for home based services can be relieved. #Winning
Each program within the MaineCare system is equally essential to the State's ability to meet the needs of its citizens. It takes the entire spectrum of services and supports to create a system where everyone can access the services and supports they need with the lowest barriers, and where their needs can best be met.
We ask that, in your good work to craft a responsible budget in the coming weeks, you keep in mind that, for the sake of a strong direct care workforce, we must prioritize competitive compensation and benefits (think: COLAs), but also consider the budget implications for access to housing that is affordable, transportation that is readily available, child care that is safe and accessible, and care for older adults that is responsive -- all are essential to sustaining a strong workforce. These people are the very foundation within the continuum of health care, long term care, home care, personal care, programs for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, programs for people living with physical disabilities and brain injuries, and all the programs that create wellness and safety for those we all serve. They deserve to be prioritized and valued in this budget, as they are in our programs.
Thank you for your consideration and for your service to our State and its citizens.

LeadingAge ME NH and its members stand ready to support your work, at your request. dvachon@leadingagemenh.org

Elizabeth Trehu Vienna LD 2212
Senator Ingwerson, Representative Meyer, Senator Grohoski, Representative Gattine, and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services: my name is Dr. Elizabeth Trehu and I live in Vienna. I am here today to testify neither for nor against LD 2212." I am a retired hematologist-oncologist who has seen first hand the devastation experienced by cancer patients and their families when the cost of their care depletes all their savings.
You have all heard the myth of the trickle down economy, the idea that giving more money to the rich will result in better lives for the rest of us as they stimulate the economy. I'm writing today about "trickle up economic destruction," when cuts impacting the poorest in our communities result in devastation that reaches far up into the middle class.
Cuts and work requirements for healthcare in HR1 could take away health insurance from 30,000 Mainers, many of whom live in rural areas. That leads to decreased funding and reimbursement to hospitals and doctors, and will result in job losses, hospital closures, and loss of essential services and life-saving care, especially in rural areas. Young people won't want to move to an area without maternity services, retirees won't want to live multiple hours from the nearest hospitals, and the result is declining populations in Maine's many rural communities, which are already struggling. People who can afford to, including doctors and other highly trained healthcare professionals will move, often out of state, leaving the most needy behind with no services.
The only solution is for the wealthiest in the state to fill the gap created by the federal budget cuts. I used to live in Massachusetts, where everyone predicted that the wealth tax would drive wealthy people and companies away from Massachusetts. The opposite happened. Wealthy people need the goods and services provided by a healthy economy to live, and when the middle class thrives, everyone benefits. Someone making over a million dollars a year is not going to feel the loss of a few tens of thousands of dollars that could make life saving differences for the rest of us.
I urge you to raise the revenue to provide Mainers with decent healthcare by making the wealthiest pay their fair share.

Gus Dunn Hindle Maine People's Alliance LD 2212
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, Senator Ingwerson, Representative Meyer, and Honorable members of the Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services, My name is Gus Dunn-Hindle, and I am the legislative strategist for Maine People's Alliance, speaking on behalf of our 32,000 members across the state of Maine.
Our mission is to create a world where everyone has what they need, contributes what they can, and no one is left behind.
I am here today to testify neither for nor against LD 2212.
Following federal funding cuts, people's health insurance costs are skyrocketing. According to the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), 31,000 Mainers across the state are at risk of losing their healthcare entirely. With less revenue from insurance payments and direct assistance, hospitals and other health care providers are at risk of closing, leaving people without access to life-saving care, especially in rural areas. This is essential infrastructure that would be far easier to keep open than to rebuild. Hospital closures and increased costs mean fewer jobs and less spending from normal households, which will be disastrous for Maine's economy, where health care is one of the largest employment sectors.
These cuts, which according to DHHS, will result in "long-term health consequences including premature death," were made to pay for $1 Trillion in tax cuts for corporations and the richest 1%. This is not a question of belt-tightening to make it through hard times, it is simply a move to pad the pockets of the already-rich at the cost of our health as a state and as a nation.
Fortunately, Maine doesn't have to accept this state of affairs. We urge you to support any and all opportunities to fully fund and expand MaineCare, and to provide funding to support health care providers at risk of closing, families facing increasing health insurance costs, and people who have lost their health insurance entirely.
These measures will require spending, but it is spending that is absolutely necessary to the health of Maine's people and economy. By raising revenue from the ultra-wealthy and corporations who benefit from the federal cuts, we can make the necessary investments without hurting ordinary Mainers. We need to raise revenue from those corporations and ultra-wealthy Mainers to fund the services and save the hospitals, jobs, and lives that the federal government is willing to sacrifice.
LD 1089, 1879, and 229 are bills currently before the legislature that would raise roughly $215 million in revenue from ultra-wealth individuals and corporations making over $3.5 Million in profits, while lowering the tax rate for 70% of Mainers. This would bring us within striking distance of backfilling these disastrous cuts and ensuring that all Mainers have access to health care. On behalf of our members, I urge you to reject the sacrifice of ordinary people for the private accumulation of vast amounts of wealth. We have an opportunity to stop the destruction caused by these cuts, and to build towards a future where every Mainer has access to high-quality health care. We are asking the honorable committee members to rise to the moment and meet that opportunity. Thank you very much.
Gus Dunn Hindle Maine People's Alliance gus@mainepeoplesalliance.org
