Dear Members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee,
My name is Stacia Brough, and I am a 44-year-old mother of four from Norway, Maine. I am here to speaAk in favor of LD 2212.
Before I found the support and opportunities that helped change my path, my life looked very different. I became pregnant with my first child at 17 and dropped out of school during my junior year to care for him. Two years later, my daughter was born. Being a struggling single mother was one of the hardest challenges of my life. Back in 2000, I was living on just $550 a month from TANF assistance, while my rent was $475.There were times when I could not even afford diapers. I knew if I wanted to provide for my children, I needed an education. At that point in my life, I was just trying to survive; I did not even think thriving was a possibility in my situation. It is hard to get ahead when you are living in survival mode . In rural communities like where I am from, this is the reality for many people; opportunities feel out of reach. Public transportation is almost nonexistent, jobs are often part-time or pay a very low wage, and accessing higher education means traveling long distances, something that is not realistic for many parents without reliable vehicles, childcare, or flexible work schedules. For families living paycheck to paycheck, even the cost of gas can be a barrier to attending classes.
Adult education, community colleges, and workforce development programs are vital to rural Maine. These programs provide more than just classes; they offer second chances. The adult education program at OHCHS helped me secure my first job and begin rebuilding my confidence. The program offered both day and night classes, allowing me to attend while being the sole caregiver for my children. I graduated in 2011 and immediately enrolled in a CNA course at our local high school, allowing me to start working right away. These community-based programs were accessible, free, and specifically designed for working adults, making it possible for me to participate.
When I began working, it felt incredibly rewarding, but unfortunately, I was still only earning minimum wage. I started at $7.50 an hour, and after a few years, I was still only making $10.00 an hour. I would not have made it through this period in my life without subsidized housing. I realized that if I wanted to truly change my family's future, I needed more education and better credentials.
Workforce development programs are critical to rural Maine because they are built around accessibility. Many now offer online or hybrid courses, which are essential in areas where transportation is a major barrier. When you live miles from the nearest campus, and there is no bus system, online learning can mean the difference between continuing your education and giving up. Being able to complete coursework from home allows parents like me to study after putting our children to bed, without worrying about how we will get to class or who will watch the kids.
The cost of living continues to rise; housing, heating oil, groceries, and childcare are all expensive, especially in rural areas like mine, with few jobs and low wages. When residents have the opportunity to earn degrees or certifications, they are more likely to secure stable, higher-paying jobs and remain in their communities. Most of the people who pursue education through local or online programs secure work, and they do not leave; they stay. They buy homes, pay property taxes, support local businesses, and reinvest their earnings back into the local economy. Investing in education is not just an investment in individuals; it is an investment in Maine's workforce, small towns, and long-term economic stability.
In 2024 began by taking a workforce development course at WCCC, where I earned my MHRT/C certification. Programs like this are especially important in rural Maine because they train local residents to fill high-need roles in healthcare, teaching, and social services fields that are desperately needed in our communities. Instead of

importing workers from outside the region, these programs empower people who already live here to serve their own communities.
After completing the workforce course, I felt more confident about pursuing my degree. That confidence is one of the most powerful outcomes of adult education and workforce development. It is not just about job training; it is about self-worth, stability, and hope. Now, I am working on a degree in forensic social work. My goal is to give back to the same kinds of communities and families who face the challenges I once did.
Education strengthens communities in ways that go beyond just increasing a person's income. Research consistently shows that higher levels of education are linked to lower crime rates and reduced substance use. When people have access to opportunity, stable employment, and hope for the future, communities become safer and healthier. Maine needs to invest in its people, especially in rural areas, where people are struggling to stay afloat. By expanding access to affordable, flexible education programs, we can reduce poverty, lower crime and drug rates, and build stronger, more resilient communities for the next generation of Mainers.
If we want to keep young people in Maine, we have to invest in their education and futures. More and more young adults are leaving the state because they see that there are better opportunities elsewhere. When Maine expands workforce training, online degree programs, and career pathways tied to local industries, it gives young people a reason to stay. If they can earn credentials close to home and find meaningful, sustainable employment in their own communities, they are more likely to build their lives here, start families, purchase homes, and contribute to the future of our dying towns.
Keeping young people in Maine is vital to strengthening our workforce, rebuilding our communities, supporting our aging population, and preserving the character and vitality of rural communities. These education programs are affordable, flexible, and accessible through online options and are not luxuries. These programs are lifelines and provide a way out of poverty, while strengthening the local workforce and keeping families rooted in their communities. Without these programs, many of us would never have the opportunity to move from surviving to thriving.
Sincerely, Stacia Brough

10060353:
Stephanie Fraone Scarborough LD 2212
Dear Committee,
Like many parents, educators, and health professionals, I am deeply concerned about the impact of social media on our children's developing minds and mental health. However, I would like to focus here on an equally pressing concern within this landscape: the role that smartphones and mobile devices play in disrupting the learning process itself.
Research shows that mobile devices serve as distractions in the classroom - even when out of sight in a backpack or pocket. Because these devices are designed to capture attention, our brains have essentially been trained to anticipate and shift focus with every ping, vibration, or silent notification from a text message or social media app. A student (or anyone for that matter) does not need to be actively checking their phone/device to be distracted. Instead, the brain remains in a state of alertness which divides attention and increases cognitive load. In effect, they are multitasking just by having the device nearby/accessible. This undermines concentration and can impair working memory, which is the system responsible for initially holding and manipulating information. When working memory is disrupted, so is the flow of information into short-term memory and, ultimately, long-term memory. Why does this matter? When this process is disrupted repeatedly throughout the day, research has shown that students are less able to absorb new material, follow complex instruction, or build on prior knowledge. Over time, these small interruptions can translate into lower academic performance, weaker retention of core concepts, and widening gaps in learning.
Device usage during the school day does not affect all students equally. Students with attention or executive functioning challenges, such as ADHD or anxiety, are especially vulnerable to distraction. Additionally, students experience different levels of dependency on their devices, and for some, that dependency can significantly interfere with attention, impulse control, and ultimately, learning. A consistent, schoolwide approach to device usage supports all students, especially those who need structure and fewer distractions in order to learn effectively.
Couple all of this with the burden placed on teachers to manage device-related disruptions in the classroom; it doesn't affect just one student it interrupts the learning process for everyone. Critically, research shows that it can take students anywhere from 5 to over 20 minutes to fully refocus on academic tasks after a distraction, depending on the complexity of the task. Each small distraction can add up quickly, resulting in a substantial loss of instructional time and disruption of students' ability to process and retain information. This isn't unique to school. We see similar patterns in the workplace, where each distraction or need to context switch reduces productivity. In the school setting, productivity is our students' learning.
More recently, national assessment data shows clear and concerning learning deficits among U.S. students. Unfortunately, Maine is no exception. We have a responsibility to foster the most effective and equitable learning environments possible. One evidence-based way that we can play a role is by effectively managing mobile device usage in schools. Creating consistent policies to minimize unnecessary distractions can help give our students the best opportunity to focus, learn, and succeed.
Thank you for your time and for considering this line of evidence as you shape policy that supports our students.
Sincerely, Stephanie Fraone, PhD (Cognitive and Perceptual Psychology) Parent of a middle school child, Maine

To Whom It May Concern,
My name is Susan Zych. I have worked as a Registered Nurse for 44 years, the last 24 as a school nurse. I would like to make a counterpoint to the argument that students need to have a cell phone in school in case they need to contact their parent(s).
In this situation a responsible student woke up with a headache but insisted he was well enough to go to school because he didn't want to miss his classes. By mid-morning the student felt worse and texted his mom to come pick him up. Mom responded that she was at work and would be able to pick him up at lunchtime. The student went to his next two classes and while he was at lunch his mom arrived to pick him up.
The next morning mom contacted the nurse to let her know her son was diagnosed with the flu. From the time this student texted his mom he unknowingly exposed the eight students within the 6 foot radius of his desk in each of his two classes, the five students within the 6 foot radius of his cafeteria seat and any other student or staff member he spoke with face to face.
I cannot fault this student for exposing over 20 members of the school community to the flu. In his defense all he was trying to do was not miss any of his classes. The problem was the school policy that allowed this student to use his cell phone between classes and circumvent being seen in the nurse's office. If he did not have access to his cell phone he would have been assessed by the school nurse and isolated from other students and staff, thus minimizing the spread of the flu.
Did this student's mom need to be contacted? Yes, absolutely. Was there another option to contact his mom without jeopardizing the health and wellbeing of the school community? Yes, absolutely.
COVID, the flu and multiple other viruses are here to stay. We now have outbreaks of the measles in several states. During the COVID pandemic we learned we can control the spread of these infectious diseases in our schools. But we cannot control the spread of diseases we do not know about. Students being allowed to carry cell phones during school `in case they need to contact their parents' inhibits our ability to control the spread of infectious diseases.

Dear Members of the Committee,
I am writing in support of including bell-to-bell cell phone bans in Maine's supplemental budget. This is a necessary step to protect students and ensure a healthy, focused learning environment across the state.
We cannot leave this issue up to individual school districts. While local control is important especially here in Maine, health concerns must take priority. A patchwork of inconsistent policies will only continue to leave many students unprotected and many educators unsupported.
Maine has faced issues like this before. When the health and safety of children are at stake, we do not rely on voluntary or district-by-district decision-making. We have used statewide policy to address major student health concerns--such as concussion protocols, smoking restrictions, and other school safety standards--because consistent protections matter.
To be clear: this is a health issue. Smartphones in schools pose serious risks due to their addictive design--driven by constant notifications, social media feedback loops, and algorithmic content. Exposure to cyberbullying functions as an independent risk factor for depression and suicidality in youth. The product design of social media algorithms exploit children and undermine students' mental, emotional, and physical health.
Unrestricted access during the school day leads to chronic distraction, inability to focus, disrupts learning and sleep patterns, increases anxiety and depression through social comparison, and reduces essential face-to-face social interaction. The compulsive urge to check devices hijacks attention and fosters dependency patterns similar to behavioral addictions. Personal mobile phones and digital products present disciplinary and educational challenges--as well as serious health concerns.

This isn't about local versus state control. Our statewide efforts are about keeping Mainers in charge of Maine classrooms. This is keeping control in Maine instead of giving control to Big Tech. Without coordinated statewide action, Maine students lose. This is the same for other states. For states to retain control against Big Tech, they must coordinate statewide action.
I urge you to support bell-to-bell phone-free school policies through the supplemental budget and ensure that all Maine students have the same protections and the same opportunity to learn without digital interference.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Thom Partridge, Scarborough, ME

Good afternoon, Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Agriculture, Conversation, and Forestry. My name is Alex Carter (she/her), and I am a Senior Policy Advocate at Maine Equal Justice, a nonprofit civil legal aid provider working to increase economic security, opportunity, and equity for people in Maine. I'm testifying today neither for nor against language part F-1 for emergency food funding in the Governor's supplemental budget.
This fall, we saw the foreshadowing of a hunger crisis in our state when the federal government threatened to withhold Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefit payments from states during the longest government shutdown. Like many of you, we received hundreds of calls and messages from Mainers who were frightened about where their next meal would come from and how they would choose between buying food and paying their rent or heating bill should their SNAP benefits lapse. Overnight, we saw increased demand at food pantries as people prepared for the worst and many pantries quickly became overwhelmed and unable to keep up.
Thankfully, for the nearly 170,000 Mainers who relied on SNAP, the Governor was able to use state contingency funds to support our emergency food network, and the shutdown ended before our state agencies needed to prorate or delay SNAP benefit payments. However, the experience provided a cautionary lesson-if and when the federal government abdicates its responsibilities and violates the law, Maine must be prepared to act quickly to ensure that our residents can meet their most basic needs. We cannot allow food for our neighbors to become a political bargaining chip.

We support the proposed amendment to the existing Maine Budget Stabilization Fund statute, MRSA �1532, sub-�9 in Part F-1. The change updates the amount the Governor is allowed to release to nonprofit entities providing food from $400,000 to $4,000,000 during a declared state of emergency. This better reflects the scope of need that our state-wide network of food pantries experience in an emergency, such as a natural disaster or the most recent federal government shutdown, and would serve to keep more shelves stocked and more families fed.
However, while this is an important initiative for stabilizing the charitable food network in times of increased food insecurity, food pantries cannot and should not fill the gap left by SNAP. We often hear from our clients and leadership members with young children or from older adults and people with disabilities that food banks are not easily accessible to them and lack of transportation, limited hours, and dietary needs pose additional barriers. Some of our pantry partners report they have seen a steep drop-off amongst immigrants who are no longer accessing food cites for fear of being targeted or profiled by immigration agents. SNAP benefits also support local economies, especially in rural areas, and when SNAP funding is cut or withheld small businesses like grocery stores and family farms also suffer losses.
To that end, we recommend expanding the language and allowable amount in Part F1 to allow for stabilization funds to be loaded to EBT cards for replacement SNAP benefits during a declared state of emergency. These changes would not impact the budget baseline but would act as an insurance policy should we face another crisis.
In a time when food prices and food insecurity are on the rise in Maine,1 and the cost of living is becoming more unaffordable for everyday Mainers, we need programs like SNAP to help families make ends meet and to keep our local economies afloat. We also need contingency plans and emergency flexibilities as the federal government continues to sow chaos and undercut our vital federal-state partnerships.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify and I would be happy to answer any questions.

Anna Nasset Concerned Citizen/Victim of Crime LD 2212 Good morning. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today.
I am Anna Nasset, and I am here to share my personal experience as a victim of stalking. I strongly urge action to implement a statewide automated victim notification system in Maine. Although I currently reside out of state, my connection and deep concern for victim safety in Maine remain strong, as I resided here for many years.
As a victim and survivor of stalking for the last fifteen years, the issue of automated victim notification is incredibly important for my safety.
My ordeal involves a stranger and serial stalker, Fraser Rotchford, who has a diagnosis of schizophrenia. He began targeting me in 2008 or 2009. It started when I owned an art gallery in Washington State, and the offender wanted to show his artwork. Unbeknownst to me initially, he also believes we are married, sometimes wants to kill me, and had been watching me for years. He began to torment my life with messaging, following me, and threats.
In 2012, he served 364 days in jail for misdemeanor harassment. By the end of 2013, I closed my beloved business due to his relentless behavior. In 2019, I returned to Washington to testify at his trial. My stalker was found guilty of aggravated felony stalking and felony cyber-stalking and was sentenced to the maximum of 10 years in prison--at the time, one of the longest sentences for stalking in our country's history.
Stalking is a terrifying and psychological crime. The effects of being a victim are a lifelong sentence. Being a victim of crime was a full-time job that began unexpectedly in 2011. It is now a part-time job where I'm always on call--a job I don't get to quit.
Since my offender is incarcerated in Washington state, I relied on their notification system, specifically VINE, to keep me informed. In 2012 a police officer made me aware of VINE. Thankfully almost every agency involved, from police officers to the Department of Corrections (DOC), shared VINE with me.
My experience with VINE has been life changing. I called VINE and spoke with a live person, trained and trauma-informed, who walked me through the system and reassured me. I would be notified immediately if the offender was released on bail. Over the years, VINE has consistently notified me immediately when there has been a change in status.

Offices in Augusta, Bangor, Lewiston, Biddeford and Presque Isle LSE Helpline 1-800-750-5353 (Voice/TTY) www.mainelse.org

Legal Services for Maine Elders February 23, 2026 Page 2
My name is John Brautigam, and I submit this testimony on behalf of Legal Services for Maine Elders (LSE). LSE is a statewide nonprofit civil legal aid organization focused on protecting the basic human needs of older Mainers when those needs are in jeopardy.
I. About Legal Services for Maine Elders
Through our Helpline and direct representation, we help people navigate serious civil legal problems involving housing stability, access to benefits and health coverage, consumer and financial exploitation, serious financial and personal abuse, and other matters where the loss of rights or autonomy can quickly become a crisis.
To give the Committees a high-level sense of LSE's capacity and impact, in 2025 our Helpline received 13,328 calls, and we opened 5,079 legal matters serving 4,182 clients statewide. Even at that volume, we still had to turn away hundreds of eligible callers because our capacity is finite. Our matters reflect the real-world pressures older Mainers with low incomes face: housing (about 26% of matters), self-determination such as wills and powers of attorney (about 26%), consumer problems (about 17%), health (about 15%), benefits (about 5%), along with family and individual rights. Across all matters, 82% of our cases resulted in an improved or favorable outcome, and less than one percent resulted in a not improved or unfavorable outcome.
Legal Services for Maine Elders is one part of Maine's broader civil legal aid network. That network includes multiple providers whom you will hear from today, all serving distinct needs across the state, and this funding supports coordinated capacity across that network. LSE's role in that network focuses on older Mainers with low incomes and few assets. We also provide extensive assistance with complex Medicare issues, including the Part D prescription drug benefit program. We coordinate with partner organizations such as the Area Agencies on Aging and utilize other referral pathways. But when a highly specialized legal problem erupts on an urgent basis, the alternatives are limited.
The people we serve are often unseen, unheard, and at-risk. Without help, they suffer alone and in silence. An eviction notice, a utility disconnection, an improper denial of benefits, an abusive debt collection effort, or a suspicious transfer of property can arrive quickly and accelerate on legal timelines that do not pause for a person's age, health, or income.
II. The Imperative of Civil Legal Services Funding
LSE supports adding $3 million to the Civil Legal Services Fund Commission to sustain and strengthen Maine's statewide civil legal aid network and maintain service levels.
LSE is profoundly grateful for the Legislature's $3 million supplemental investment in civil legal aid for FY 2025-26. That support translated immediately into real help for real people across Maine. It is precisely because that investment is working, and because the continuing need is so immediate, that we are back before you today to ask that funding be sustained through the second year of the biennium.

Legal Services for Maine Elders February 23, 2026 Page 3
Legal service providers who received a share of the $3 million investment for the first year of the biennium are hard at work deploying those funds to meet critical and growing needs statewide. The problem is the second year of the biennium. Unless the Legislature acts, we face a funding cliff in FY 2026-27. That drop would force reduced services in every county and would mean more Mainers trying to cope alone with legal crises of every type.
This is a statewide capacity request. It is not limited to one provider, one region, or one category of civil legal need. It is an investment in the infrastructure that allows Maine people with low incomes to protect housing, health, safety, and income when civil legal problems arise and when the legal system is already in motion. The Civil Legal Services Fund Commission is the right vehicle for this investment because it supports coordinated, proven, accountable statewide capacity across providers.
III. Measurable results
When civil legal aid capacity drops, the effects are not abstract. If the $3 million is not sustained, thousands fewer Mainers will receive legal help next year. Every county will see reduced service capacity, with the greatest impact in rural areas. Those reductions translate into fewer staffed helpline hours, fewer attorneys able to accept cases, longer waits, and more people forced to handle serious civil legal problems alone. All civil legal service providers closely track our cases and their outcomes, and extensive detailed information is available upon request.
This is also a courts-and-dockets issue. When more people must proceed without counsel, cases take longer and are harder to resolve. More unrepresented litigants strain dockets and delay proceedings. Adequate civil legal aid capacity helps courts by improving the quality of filings, clarifying issues earlier, increasing the likelihood of durable resolutions, and reducing avoidable continuances that come from confusion rather than merit. Access to justice is not only an individual right but also part of how the civil legal system functions efficiently and fairly.
IV. Civil legal aid stabilizes basic needs before problems become crises
For older Mainers with low incomes, stability often depends on essentials: safe housing, heat and electricity, access to health care, and protection from fraud or exploitation. When one of those essentials is threatened, the legal system must be there to provide a resolution.
Civil legal aid is Maine's frontline capacity for meeting those problems early, before they become crises. We help people keep housing and avoid unlawful displacement, prevent or remedy improper utility shutoffs, protect income streams that pay for food and medication, address predatory or unlawful debt collection, resolve benefits problems that create cascading instability, and intervene when a vulnerable person is financially exploited. This legal work supports outcomes with fiscal and human benefits throughout state government and the community-based system: fewer people forced into emergency shelter, fewer avoidable hospitalizations, fewer unsafe living situations, and fewer problems that become far more expensive to unwind later.

Legal Services for Maine Elders February 23, 2026 Page 4
V. Why this investment is the smart approach
This request is not simply about "more funding." It is about avoiding an unnecessary contraction in statewide capacity and dismantling of infrastructure. The question before the Legislature is whether Maine will sustain a proven, deployed investment in access to justice through the second year of the biennium, or whether civil legal aid capacity will shrink abruptly at the moment it is most needed.
Today in early 2026 many Maine households are under increasing financial pressure, and public benefit programs are stretched to the breaking point. Systems are under strain, and administrative barriers, denials, terminations, and red tape increase the demand for legal help. The state's civil legal aid network is often the last practical resource standing between a problem and a crisis.
VI. The request
For these reasons, Legal Services for Maine Elders respectfully joins with all the civil legal service providers and those who care about fair and equitable access to justice urging you to add $3 million in FY 2026-27 to the Civil Legal Services Fund to sustain Maine's statewide civil legal aid network and support our clients in their hour of need.
Thank you for your time and for your work on behalf of Maine people.

Final Words
These stories illustrate where systems fail those who are at risk, and the cascade of consequences if the breakdown is not addressed. A single administrative error or missed notice can quickly become irreversible and lead to emergency shelter use, untreated medical needs, avoidable hospitalizations, unnecessary guardianship, prolonged abuse, and long-term instability. LSE is a front-line stabilizer that interrupts that cascade.
We do not solve every problem. In those cases where legal relief is not possible, representation still produces public value: informed acceptance rather than fear, a plan rather than paralysis, and prevention rather than repetition. Clients learn how to avoid the same trap next month or next year, and that information spreads through their communities, improving outcomes beyond any one individual case.
With continued public support, LSE will be there for all these clients and thousands more.
Justice is best and most effectively served when all parties in legal disputes are competently represented by counsel. The many ways in which lawyers help their clients understand and participate in the pursuit of justice help assure the fair, prompt, and practical resolution of disputes. When the benefits of representation are missing, public confidence in the judicial system is reduced and our most vulnerable residents may be set adrift at crucial times in their lives. Providing representation at those critical points improves not just the fairness and understanding of the outcomes, but may reduce costs to all involved, including the taxpayers. Maine's Judicial Branch wholeheartedly supports maximizing the availability of legal counsel for those who cannot otherwise afford representation.
- Leigh Saufley, Chief Justice, Maine Supreme Judicial Court, 2016

Testimony of Nell Brimmer Executive Director, Maine Volunteer Lawyers Project
Joint Standing Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and esteemed members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee; Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and esteemed members of the Judiciary Committee:
My name is Nell Brimmer, and I serve as Executive Director of the Maine Volunteer Lawyers Project (VLP). VLP's mission is to connect dedicated volunteer attorneys with individuals in need of civil legal assistance, ensuring equal access to justice statewide. Our vision is that all Mainers who require civil legal help can obtain expert, timely assistance regardless of their ability to pay.
VLP operates within Maine's coordinated statewide civil legal aid system, designed to ensure that lowincome Mainers can access representation regardless of geography. The seven providers supported through the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund function within a structured framework that promotes collaboration, minimizes duplication, and deploys limited resources efficiently across the state. This coordinated model is essential to preserving meaningful access to justice for vulnerable households.
Within that framework, VLP expands the system's reach by providing the structure, coordination, and professional support that enable attorneys to deliver high-quality pro bono representation to individuals who would otherwise have no access to counsel. In doing so, we strengthen communities and support the fair administration of justice.
The supplemental budget before you will determine whether current civil legal aid capacity can be sustained. We respectfully urge the Committee to include $3 million in the FY 2026-2027 supplemental budget, in addition to the existing $1.3 million baseline for the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund. Without this funding, the expiration of last year's one-time appropriation will result in a substantial reduction in civil legal aid capacity beginning July 1, 2026. Across the statewide network, this will mean loss of critical staffing, reduced intake and clinic capacity, and fewer Mainers served--leaving more individuals to navigate complex and disruptive legal challenges without support.
When demand for civil legal assistance increases, civil legal aid provides stability. It prevents crises from escalating, supports the fair and orderly resolution of disputes, and helps ensure that Maine's courts function effectively and efficiently. This request is not for expansion; it is to maintain current capacity within the state's coordinated civil legal aid system and to avoid service reductions that will affect households across the state.
For these reasons, we respectfully urge the Committee to include $3 million in the supplemental budget for the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund.
Thank you for your consideration.
75 Pearl St, Portland, ME 04101|PO Box 2312 Bangor, ME 04402-2312

Testimony in Opposition / With Serious Concerns
LD 2212 - Supplemental Budget (Emergency) Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee
I am submitting testimony regarding LD 2212, the Governor's supplemental budget.
Supplemental budgets are intended to address unforeseen or limited shortfalls. They are not intended to normalize structural imbalance or recurring expenditure patterns that exceed available revenue.
When the State brings forward an emergency supplemental budget, it signals that projections, allocations, or internal financial controls did not align with actual expenditures. That should concern all of us.
Before additional appropriations are approved, the Legislature should require:
� A clear accounting of current General Fund balances � Updated revenue projections � Identification of whether shortfalls are one-time or structural � A detailed explanation of any departments requesting recurring increases � Disclosure of any unresolved audit findings or accounting irregularities
If the books are not fully reconciled and transparent, approving additional spending only compounds the problem.
An emergency designation requires a two-thirds vote. That threshold exists for a reason. Emergency status should be reserved for true and immediate fiscal necessity -- not administrative convenience or ongoing budget drift.
Maine citizens expect balanced budgets, responsible stewardship, and full transparency before additional taxpayer dollars are committed.
This Legislature should insist on clear financial reconciliation and structural reform before expanding or backfilling spending.
Respectfully submitted,
Wendy L. Fenderson Limerick, Maine

Members of the Appropriations & Financial Affairs Committee and the Veterans & Legal
Affairs Committee, thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today. My name is Eric
Campbell, and I serve as a Captain with the Maine Air National Guard Fire Department. I am
here on my personal time to request that all members of your committees work to ensure funding for An Act to Address Employee Retention of State Employees Who Are Firefighters at Bangor Intemational Airport, as part of the Governor's proposed Supplemental Budget, LD 2212

I have been a State of Maine employee for more than 24 years, begimiing my career with the
Department of Corrections before becoming a State Firefighter in 2007. I also retired from the
101st Air Refueling Wing after 22 years of service in the Maine National Guard, including 18 years as a firefighter and five overseas deployments.
`
Under the current retirement structure, firefighters must complete 25 years of service and reach
`
age 55 to retire without penalty. LD 1236 would remove the age-55 requirement and allow retirement at 50% after 25 years of service, with no minimum age. For someone like me---
approaching 25 years of service--retiring at age 50 would result in a 15% penalty, simply for not meeting the age threshold. This penalty forces many firefighters to continue working well past the point when the physical demands of the job remain safe or sustainable.

Firefighting is uniquely strenuous work. Years of emergency responses, hands-on training,
physical fitness requirements, disrupted sleep cycles, and exposure to toxic enviromnents take a
cumulative toll on the body. Our protective gear itself contains PFAS, adding another layer of
long-term health risk. Many members of the Maine ANG Fire Department spend their entire
careers in frontline roles, and the physical strain compounds year after year.

For those who begin their careers around age 20, the current system effectively requires 35 years
of frontline firefighting duties. That level of physical endurance becomes increasingly
unrealistic--and unsafe--as firefighters age. I am now old enough to be the father of many of our firefighters, and in fact, I am the father of one of them. The idea that firefighters must remain
in these roles until age 55, regardless of physical wear, is simply not aligned with the realities of
the profession.

LD 1236 has already passed both the Senate and the House. State Firefighters are asking for
parity with the State Police and State Fire Investigators, who already have no minimum age
requirement. This change would also support retention. We have already lost several firefighters

to departments offering better retirement programs, and this bill would help us remain

competitive. The cost to the State is minimal--an initial one-time funding charge--while all

I3

future funding is fully reimbursed by the federal govermnent under our Master Cooperative

l

Agreement.
Q
1

On behalf of our entire department, I respectfully ask for your support to ensure that LD 1236

k

moves forward this session and is not carried over again.

Thank you for your time and for your continued service to the people of Maine.

Eric Campbell

Testimony from the Crew

We are the men and women who build and maintain this state.

We are the ones on the highways before sunrise, under bridges in the freezing wind, on scaffolding in the summer heat when the asphalt sticks to our boots. We pourthe
concrete, weld the steel, repair the roads, and keep the infrastructure standing so that
everyone else can safely get to work, school, and home to their families.

We are proud of what we do.

T

We are proud that when storms hit, we show up.
When something collapses, we rebuild it. When deadlines seem impossible, we work the extra hours to meet them.

Many of us log 250 or more hours of overtime every season. Not because we want to live at work -- but because we have to.

Despite the long hours, despite the physical toll on our bodies, despite missing birthdays,
ball games, anniversaries, and family dinners -- too many of us are still living paycheck to
paycheck.

Every day on the job site, the same conversations happen: "Did you see your grocery bill this week?"
"My rent went up again."
"l had to put the heating bill on a credit card."
"| don't know how l'm going to afford my kid's braces."
These aren't stories from people who don't work hard. These are stories from people who work 50, 60, sometimes 70 hours a week.
We are not asking for luxury. We are asking for stability.
We are asking to be able to pay our bills without panic.
*
To fill our gas tanks without calculating what will bounce. To buy groceries without putting items back at the register. To take care of our families without sacrificing our health and every waking hour of our lives.
The cost of living keeps rising -- food, housing, utilities, healthcare -- everything. But our wages are not keeping up. The gap between what we earn and what it takes to live grows
wider every year.

The truth is this job takes a toll.

Our backs ache. Our knees give out. Our shoulders carry years of wear and tear.
We work through injuries because the work has to get done.
And we do it willingly-- because we believe in the importance of what we build.
But dedication should not mean desperation.
Working overtime used to mean getting ahead. Now itjust means keeping up. And even
with 250+ overtime hours, many of us are barely staying afloat.
We are the backbone of this state's infrastructure. Without our labor, projects stop. Roads go unrepaired. Public works stall. Communities suffer. We take pride in knowing that what
we build lasts for generations.
All we are asking is that our livelihoods last too.
We want to continue doing this work with pride -- not with constant financial anxiety. We want to retire one day with dignity. We want our families to feel secure, not stressed every
time the mail arrives.
This isn'tjust about numbers on a contract. lt's about people. lt's about families. lt's about fairness.
We are not disposable. We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for compensation that reflects the reality of today's cost of living and the
value of the work we perform every single day.
We show up. We put in the hours. We carry this state on our backs.
All we're asking is forthe chance to stand on solid ground ourselves.

Good Morning Senator Rotundo and Representative Gattine, Senator Baldacci and Representative Salisbury, and esteemed members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee and the State and Local Government Committee.
My name is Luke Shorty and I reside in Winthrop, Maine and am the Immediate Past Chair of Volunteer Maine, Maine's Commission for Community Service.
Volunteer Maine addresses critical needs in the state, particularly rural and underserved communities, through service and volunteerism. In 2025, Volunteer Maine delivered more than $2 million in grants and contracts directly benefiting communities across Maine. Despite a challenging federal funding environment, the Commission remained focused in delivering in its core mission: to promote excellence in volunteer management, strengthen civic infrastructure, and ensure that service remains embedded as a problem-solving strategy across Maine's communities.
Most of the initiatives related to Volunteer Maine before you are housekeeping in nature-- technical adjustments that help ensure Volunteer Maine can continue to operate efficiently and in alignment with state requirements. There is, however, one substantive proposal that we care deeply about that is not before you and that we believe presents Maine with an important opportunity to strengthen the long-term sustainability of an institution that serves communities across our entire state.
On behalf of Volunteer Maine's Commission, I would like to request General Fund support to cover 50% of the Executive Director's salary-- $18,392 in FY26 and $74,603 in FY27. The remaining 50%--$77,549 in FY27--would continue to be supported with federal funds. While this proposal was not included in the Governor's supplemental budget, we respectfully ask the AFA Committee to consider including it.
The justification is straightforward and forward-looking. Volunteer Maine's core funding has historically relied on federal AmeriCorps dollars. However, federal funding for AmeriCorps has been volatile and is expected to decrease--or potentially be eliminated--in the coming years. At the same time, federal grant funds prohibit fundraising activities. This creates a structural challenge: the very position responsible for leading and reshaping Volunteer Maine for longterm sustainability cannot use federal funds to raise the philanthropic or diversified support that will be essential to our future.
A modest state investment (roughly a nickel per Maine citizen) in 50% of the Executive Director's salary would put Volunteer Maine in a stronger position to navigate this changing funding landscape. It would allow the Executive Director to dedicate time to building philanthropic partnerships, exploring alternative funding models, strengthening statewide civic infrastructure, and preparing for multiple future scenarios. In short, it would allow Maine to

plan deliberately--rather than reactively--for a future in which our state's community service and volunteer support systems may no longer be federally funded.
Under the Executive Director's leadership, Volunteer Maine also successfully transitioned its administrative home to the Maine Office of Community Affairs (MOCA) in October 2025. We are very pleased to be part of this dynamic office, whose mission to strengthen state-municipal partnerships closely align with Volunteer Maine's role in supporting community-based solutions. This move reinforces the opportunity before us to realign and position the Commission to sustainably serve the people of Maine for years to come.
At its core, this request is about service and civic engagement. After successfully launching the Maine Service Fellows program to serve communities in rural Maine who do not have the bandwidth or infrastructure to handle a large federal grant, making this investment in Volunteer Maine will help ensure that this in demand program can continue to grow and succeed. How, you ask? By allowing the Executive Director to find other philanthropic and alternative funding sources to support programs and partnerships that harness the energy, skills, and commitment of volunteers and service members to meet local needs. We are a force multiplier that strengthens Maine communities. We are also well positioned within MOCA. And with this strategic investment, we can keep moving forward and grow in ways we know are sustainable.
This is something we care about deeply--not simply as commissioners, but as Mainers who believe in the power of service to strengthen our communities.
Thank you for your consideration, and for your continued support of service and volunteerism across our state.

197787:
To: Joint Standing Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs
A
From: Morgan Dunton
Date: February 24, 2026
Subject: Testimony in Support of Funding to Close the State Employee Pay Gap and
Resolve Bargaining Impasse (LD 2212)
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and distinguished members of the
Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee:
My name is Morgan Dunton, and I am a resident of Rockland. Until recently, I was employed by the Maine Department of Education, having served 21 years! I am here today to urge the
Committee to prioritize using a portion of Maine's projected $248 million revenue
surplus to finally close the 14% state employee pay gap and provide the necessary resources to resolve the current bargaining impasse with MSEA-SEIU Local 1989. While
the cost of living has skyrocketed, while state employees have been pleading with this Governor, pleading with you and the last 4 legislatures to provide resources for fair,
competitive wages, what did you do? You came around and voted to take away $56 million
dollars from their salary plan by raising the attrition rate? Again? Leaving the state with only
enough money for a wage offer that doesn't even keep up with the cost of living? You can
and must do better for our beloved state of Maine.

There are state workers who qualify for SNAP. For Mainecare. There are state workers who are relying on heating assistance. These folks, my former colleagues, have been dealing with understaffing for years upon years, triggered by uncompetitive wages, and so many have been working multiple jobs to make ends meet while serving the people of this state with utter exhaustion. Many give up and leave Maine altogether.

Once upon a time, the State of Maine was the most desired employer in the state of Maine.

Salary, benefits, and working conditions were sufficient to both attract and retain

committed employees. But that is just not the case anymore. The pay scale is woefully

lacking; benefits are not keeping pace either; and working conditions are often far more

desirable elsewhere. I can attest to that better than anyone.

A A

.1

Our state agencies need dedicated workers who stay in their agencies and positions long

enough to develop expert knowledge of how the agency works and to build a relationship

with stakeholders that engenders confidence in times of crisis or need. This was never

more evident than in 2020.

i

As the English Language Arts Specialist for 16 years, I had name recognition across the state and trust fueled by confidence in my knowledge and professional skill. When schools

shuttered, I began meeting daily with teachers to assure them that we could rise to the
challenge. I listened to their needs, planned professional learning activities to meet each of those needs, and inspired confidence in our collective ability to do what our students
needed. My experience, skill, and commitment provided the calming presence most
needed in that moment.
I am the exception and not the norm. For too many, state work is a steppingstone to a
better situation. State employment is no longer competitive enough to inspire career
commitment. nor one that allows workers in their 20's, 30's and 40's to afford a home and
financially support their families. For our agencies to thrive, and our state programs to
succeed, we need to make state employment more competitive and more desirable as a
long-term career commitment. Please, close the pay gap. You have the funds to do that right now. You have the ability to make a difference and show our state workers that you appreciate the work they do and assure our Maine citizens that the programs they count on will be accessible, effective, and available. Use this surplus to set the record straight. All of Maine will be better for it.
Thank you.
197783:
Chairs and Members of the Committees,
My name is Natalie Owens, and I am here today on my own time, to urge you to use the state
government surplus to return funds to the state employee salary plan. By doing so, the state will have the ability to more adequately invest in, and lift up our support staff at the Department of
Education.
Right now, we are asking highly trained leaders to do clerical work--not because they lack commitment, but because we lack adequate support staffing. When support roles pay only $18$19 per hour, we simply cannot attract or retain the level of skill the work demands. As a result,
the work does not disappear; it shifts upward.
In my own experience, I have watched directors answer phones, process invoices, manage
scheduling logistics, and handle routine administrative tasks. This is not a matter of pride or work ethic--our leaders are deeply committed. But it is a matter of efficiency. It is the difference between working harder and working smarter.
Our directors and upper managers at the Department of Education are at the peak of their
professions. Many hold master's degrees and doctorates. They are innovative, strategic thinkers who are passionate about improving outcomes for students and communities. Yet too often,
they spend large portions of their day on minutiae that trained support professionals should be
handling.
When we underpay support staff, we do not save money--we misallocate talent. We diminish organizational effectiveness. We limit the impact of the very leaders we have worked so hard to
recruit and develop.
If the State of Maine offers wages that allow support staff to support a family--wages that reflect the responsibility and complexity of the work--we will attract and retain capable professionals. That investment will pay dividends immediately. Directors and managers will be freed to lead, to innovate, and to focus on strategic priorities rather than administrative
backlogs.
This is not simply a compensation issue. It is a workforce strategy issue. It is an efficiency issue. And ultimately, it is a leadership issue.
By lifting up our support staff, you strengthen the entire system. Please work to return the money to our salary plan with the budget surplus.
Thank you for your consideration.

Paul Caruso

Testimony
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee, my name is Paul Caruso. I am here, on my own time, to speak about chronic staffing issues and the state employee pay gap for Maine's executive branch workers, in regards to LD 2212. Please dedicate the budget surplus to executive branch worker's salary plan in LD 2212.
As a Computer Programmer for the Department of Administrative and Financial Services, I see and experience the impacts of under staffing & the state employee pay gap. I believe that this budget surplus can address these issues and help ensure that the state can properly provide high-quality healthcare under its MaineCare program.
Prior to my position with the state, I was a grateful recipient of MaineCare's services. I am proud to now work for the state, but wish for the program to be in a better position. I would love to see a MaineCare program adequately staffed and compensated so that Mainers can rely on this healthcare when needed. These committees can work to better support improvements to MaineCare services by restoring the $56 million that was taken out of the state employee salary in the most recent biennial budget. This current surplus offers a pathway to make right by state workers and public we serve.
According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistic's Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics for Portland & South Portland as of May 2024, a Computer Programmer makes an annual median wage of $119,240. Living in Portland with the same job title, I am compensated at about half of that and do not find this to be fair nor attractive to talent. I occasionally spend my weekends working at my part-time job, as an on-call parking garage attendant for the City of Portland, to help afford my living costs. I am passionate about what I do for people. However, it would be very easy for me to accept an offer to take my labor elsewhere.
Good talent could be recruited and retained for the MaineCare program by investing in executive branch workers. Using this surplus to help close the state employee pay gap is in the best interest of the program and our neighbors who rely on it.
As you will likely hear testimony of today, the MaineCare program is not the only critical service provided by passionate, but under staffed and under paid, executive branch workers. Continuing to ignore these issues by failing to incorporate the budget surplus into the State Employee personnel services budget will harm executive branch workers, damage the services they provide, and would be a failure to the Mainers who rely on these critical workers & services.
Please support dedicating the budget surplus to executive branch worker's salary plan in LD 2212. I believe this will address chronic staffing issues and the state employee pay gap. I think investing in this route is an investment in state workers & Mainers alike.
Thank you, Paul Caruso

PART D
Sec. D-1. Carrying provision; Department of the Secretary of State, Administration -- Corporations, Elections and Commissions program. Notwithstanding any provision of law to the contrary, the State Controller shall carry forward up to $750,000 in unexpended balances in the Personal Services and All Other line categories in the Department of the Secretary of State, Administration - Corporations, Elections and Commissions program, after all financial commitments for obligations and budgetary adjustments have been made, at the end of fiscal year 2025-26 to the next fiscal year, to the All Other line category in the Department of the Secretary of State, Administration - Corporations, Elections and Commissions program, to be used to continue the modernization of systems and services provided to the public. These funds do not lapse and are intended to carry until expended.
PART D
SUMMARY
This Part authorizes the State Controller to carry` forward up to $750,000 in unexpended balances in the Personal Services and All Other line categories in the Department of the Secretary of State, Administration -- Corporations, Elections and Commissions program, after all financial commitments for obligations and budgetary adjustments have been made, at the end of fiscal year 2025-26 to the next fiscal year to the All Other line category in the Department of the Secretary of State, Administration -- Corporations, Elections and Commissions program. These funds are to be used to continue the modernization of systems and services administered by the program.
We routinely see costs beyond our basic allocation in election years with high attention and turnout like
the 2026 general election. While we have often covered those after the fact with a retroactive supplemental appropriation, we are concerned that such a cycle puts unnecessary stress on the elections
system. The carryover language simply allows us to carry over unused funds (capped at $750,000) to help the Elections Division under the supervision of experienced Deputy Secretary Julie Flyrm, meet any
unanticipated costs. Given the pending potential passage of the SAVE Act or the SAVE America Act,
this may be more important than ever before in 2026. - _

Senator Rotundo, Representative Gatfine, members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee. Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and members of the State and Local
Government committee. My name is Stefanie Perry; I am here testifying on my own personal
time. Thank you for taking the time to listen to us who work at the State of Maine as you consider how to prioritize spending the state surplus.

I am proudly employed with DHHS, Office for Family Independence, and represent the MSEASEIU Local 1989, Capitol Western Chapter. I am asking for the State of Maine to add 56 million
dollars to our salary budget from the current budget surplus amount of $250 million. Our goal is to close the pay gap for State Workers by funding fair wages for all employees; this money would be a tremendous help. I would like to start by saying one obvious notion--no one works
for the state of Maine to become rich or wealthy. Every colleague I have had in my 3 roles with
the State of Maine has joined the work force to earn an honest living and support their local communities.

Utilizing these surplus funds to allow for fair wage increases will automatically improve the
services we provide to Mainers. I am an Eligibility Specialist in the long-term care unit of
Portland, Maine. We have seen great turnover and hiring challenges due to low starting wages,
and inflation. Did you know that some people in my department, state workers, qualify for the
state benefits that they administer? This is the reality for Executive Branch workers across the
state of Maine. This is not okay and we need your help.

Increasing pay means increasing retention. More retention and staff means that the most
vulnerable populations will not have to wait for critical services and care; such as Nursing
Facility benefits or SNAP benefits. Better worker retention means food on the tables of Mainers who wait and go hungry, it means faster care to those who are stuck in their homes with critical
illnesses such as dementia..

We do our best to work as quickly as possible, but understaffed departments will continue to
struggle and take additional time to complete responsibilities that directly benefit the Maine

people. This is preventable and you can help.

~

E

This is the same for public safety workers, and the BMV trying to serve the line that wraps
around the building each morning at 7AM.

I ask you to consider the improvements in quality of life for state employees if their pay increases to a livable wage. Thank you for your time and consideration on this matter.

Good Afternoon, I am Trudy Newcomb, Principal at the Edmunds Consolidated School, which is one of the 3 schools managed under the DOE, Education in the Unorganized Territories, also known as the EUT. I am here on my own time to speak about chronic staffing issues and the employee pay gap for Maine's Executive Branch workers that goes unaddressed in LD 2212. I'll speak to how it is impacting hiring and retention of staff within the EUT.
This is my 13th year as a principal in the EUT. During this time, there have been at least 3 changes in principals in the other two EUT schools, and also in the Director position in the Augusta office. I am the most senior person working at the admin level in the EUT. I have witnessed, year after year, the negative impact these turnovers have had on teachers, staff, students, and most importantly on teaching and learning.
The turnover in the Augusta office slows processes that are integral to running our schools. The connections between the EUT, the DOE, and the State of Maine, are not easy to navigate, and to be losing experienced staff to other departments/positions, slows my ability to do even the most basic things that are able to be done easily in other school districts. We desperately need to be able to retain staff in the Augusta office.
I will share an example to illustrate the impact of retention and hiring at my school. We ended last school year fully staffed, for the first time in months. In late August, I learned of staff leaving. I lost a bus driver and a special education teacher to another local district as they paid better. Another new hire could not report in due to a family issue. In October, my custodian left to join the other local district, and then I lost another Ed. Tech III in November due to a move. Most of these employees left to pursue positions with higher pay and better benefits. These gaps are not small. To illustrate- the most significant difference is between teacher pay at my school, and the next town over- which is about $5,000. I can not overcome the difference in pay and benefits to attract candidates despite our school having a great educational reputation, and staff report that were they loved working at my school.
The fact is that all other districts are also desperate for staff, and their pay and benefits are better than what we can offer. I started the school year faced with 4 vacancies- a bus driver, a grade 1/2 teacher, a grade PK/K teacher, and an ed tech III. I was forced to reassign staff within my school to the 2 teaching positions less than a week before students arrived. We have advertised over and over again this year to fill these positions, and it was only last week that I was able to fill all but the janitor position. I have been since October without a full-time custodian. I have acted as teacher, ed. tech, and custodian regularly to minimize the impact on other staff and students. Other staff pitch in as well to maintain the integrity of programs, but it all negatively impacts morale among staff, the integrity of programs, and increases overall stress throughout the building.
I returned to school today, with all positions finally filled, except the custodian position, for the first time all year. I should be ecstatic, but I know this will not be my reality when more positions open in other area districts in the next few weeks and over the summer. I will once again lose talented, experienced staff to other schools that pay better and offer better benefits unless you support funding to help close the state employee pay gap in this supplemental budget. Also please work to ensure teachers at the EUT are included in the Governor's proposed minimum salary increases for K-12 teachers.

Thank you for allowing me to address you today, and I urge you to support staff working within the EUT and other Executive Branch workers in LD 2212.

Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and committee members. My name is Amanda Roy. I am testifying on my own personal time, requesting that you all work to use the state's surplus to restore the $56 million worth of funding that was taken away from the state employee personal services budget in 2025.
Since I began my career at the MDOT-Region 4 Office in April of 2025, I have seen firsthand how the state employee pay gap and working conditions have impacted new and existing employees of the Maine Department of Transportation. In my current position of Office Associate II and working the front desk reception, I have met and had the privilege of conversing with my colleague on a daily basis. During these conversations, topics of low morale, uncompetitive wages, issues with increasingly expensive benefits are mentioned often, sometimes several times in different conversations throughout my day. Something that was unexpected for me was the longevity of employees for most, the longest in our region being over 50 years of service and for some this may be the only job that they hold. The pride that some have when they share stories of their own family's generations previously that had worked to plan, design and build the roads that we all now travel daily. I'm afraid that the trajectory we are on, with leaving state employees undercompensated, will prevent these stories from being carried on into the future. Workers feel especially down when they see consultants, hired by the state, working side by side them making substantially more money on the tax payer's dime. I have also heard the frustration of being short staffed, longer storms and low retention for established employees.
In addition, in my personal life, I'm also the extremely proud wife of a MDOT Snowfighter, who has worked for MDOT for over 4 years. I have experienced the holidays without him at our Christmas dinner table, the delayed birthdays because a snow squall went through, the exhaustion that he experiences when there's multiple storms in a week's time. I have heard the frustration rumblings of the "I don't get paid enough", etc. as he gets home from his 20-30 hour day of keeping Maine roadways open and safe for our neighbors and your constituents. We are a small family who lives well within our means because right now because we have to, it is survival. While we both work two full time jobs, there are times when we have to choose whether we pay to heat our home or put food on the table. It means making those incredibly difficult decisions to pay for medications or pay the copay to be seen by the doctor. Choices, honestly that we as state employees, should have to never face. We are closer to being on governmental benefits than we are to being a financially stable household. We are not alone.
I have seen firsthand how these compensation issues continue to impact all employees on a daily basis. As you can imagine, I take great pride in my position here at MDOT and live personally and professionally by our motto: Integrity, Competence, and Service. Our roles are essential to "Keep Maine Moving", it would be validated by having a contract and wages that

reflect that gratitude and appreciation. You all have the power to put us on the right track. We need your support. Please give us our money back so we can move to close this state employee pay gap, and restore greater pride in the work we do to keep our communities safe.

and Public Safety Committee. Andre My name is Andre Cushing, and I serve as
a Penobscot County Commissioner and President of the Maine County Commissioners Association.
l am here to highlight how Maine's counties are evolving into important regional service hubs. By providing collaborative programs, we allow
municipalities to share costs and increase professional standards, ultimately reducing the burden on local property taxpayers.
Cumberland County: A Model for Assessing
Cumberland County provides a premier example of how counties
professionalize local government functions. . Regional Assessing: The Cumberland County Assessing Department allows municipalities to contract for full-time, professional
assessing services. For example, the Town of Casco recently entered
into a contract with the county to maintain high-level service that a small
town might otherwise struggle to recruit for independently.
. Scale of Service: Their Regional Communications Center serves as the 91-1 Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) for 19 of the 28 communities in the county, demonstrating a massive scale of shared infrastructure.
Penobscot County: Pioneering Regional Fire & EMS In Penobscot County, we are leading the state in addressing the critical E1\_A_S
staffing crisis.
. First Regional District: We helped facilitate the formation of the Central Maine Highlands Fire & EMS District #1, the first of its kind in Maine. This
district serves eight towns and two townships by pooling resources into

a single sustainable service hub. This effort is continuing to evolve in
three more regions of our county
- Financial Impact: These collaborations offer massive fiscal benefits. By moving away from independent municipal departments, towns can reduce redundancy in administration and equipment. Instead of each town losing $150 to $1,800 per ambulance call, the regional district maximizes federal and state supplemental funding to stabilize
costs.
- Efficiency: We also provide regional animal control for numerous
municipalities, ensuring even the most remote residents have access to certified animal welfare enforcement without the tovvn needing to
manage an independent department.
The Fiscal Reality
These efforts are the definition of efficiency, but as we take on more
municipal-style services, the pressure on the county tax levy increases. The benefits of this collaboration is overshadow by the dysfunctional funding of county jails. many counties to cover this shortfall. As you have read this has now become
unsustainable. lf you also review the recent report from the Jail Standards
Council from LD 719 you will see the real impacts driving this need. We ask for
your support in stabilizing county funding to ensure we can keep these
regional programs affordable for our towns. Thank you for your time and your commitment to all levels of Maine government.

Good morning. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today.
I am Anna Nasset, and I am here to share my personal experience as a victim of stalking. I strongly urge action to implement a statewide automated victim notification system in Maine. Although I currently reside out of state, my connection and deep concern for victim safety in Maine remain strong, as I resided here for many years.
As a victim and survivor of stalking for the last fifteen years, the issue of automated victim notification is incredibly important for my safety.
My ordeal involves a stranger and serial stalker, Fraser Rotchford, who has a diagnosis of schizophrenia. He began targeting me in 2008 or 2009. It started when I owned an art gallery in Washington State, and the offender wanted to show his artwork. Unbeknownst to me initially, he also believes we are married, sometimes wants to kill me, and had been watching me for years. He began to torment my life with messaging, following me, and threats.
In 2012, he served 364 days in jail for misdemeanor harassment. By the end of 2013, I closed my beloved business due to his relentless behavior. In 2019, I returned to Washington to testify at his trial. My stalker was found guilty of aggravated felony stalking and felony cyber-stalking and was sentenced to the maximum of 10 years in prison--at the time, one of the longest sentences for stalking in our country's history.
Stalking is a terrifying and psychological crime. The effects of being a victim are a lifelong sentence. Being a victim of crime was a full-time job that began unexpectedly in 2011. It is now a part-time job where I'm always on call--a job I don't get to quit.
Since my offender is incarcerated in Washington state, I relied on their notification system, specifically VINE, to keep me informed. In 2012 a police officer made me aware of VINE. Thankfully almost every agency involved, from police officers to the Department of Corrections (DOC), shared VINE with me.
My experience with VINE has been life changing. I called VINE and spoke with a live person, trained and trauma-informed, who walked me through the system and reassured me. I would be notified immediately if the offender was released on bail. Over the years, VINE has consistently notified me immediately when there has been a change in status.
Despite my great success with VINE, my heart still stops when I receive a notification. However, VINE has allowed me to move past that moment of panic, access the necessary information and if needed, take action to protect myself. For victims, notifications can be the difference between life and death. At the end of the day, VINE provides me and crime victims with peace of mind.

In closing, I have considered moving back to Maine again. However, the lack of a statewide victim notification system prevents me from taking that step. I ask today that you please move forward to protect victims and support a statewide automated victim notification system in Maine.
Thank you for hearing my testimony today.

Our job in the Judiciary Committee and this Legislature is to protect victims. Maine is the only state in the nation without a statewide automated victim notification system. With the time lag inherent to our
current paper notification system, many victims of crime may feel unsafe or insecure not knowing
whether their perpetrator is incarcerated or has returned to their community.
This bill is an opportunity for the State to act now to provide victims with a greater sense of security by
making accessible immediate information about changes to the status of perpetrators of crimes. Victims, law enforcement officers, family members, concerned citizens, and judges could choose to be alerted electronically via text, email, phone, or teletypewriter when an offender is released or transferred. While these notifications are for any crime, they are particularly critical for domestic violence and sexual assault survivors who, research indicates, worry most about revictimization.
After the initial hearing on LD 981, a work group was created to ensure all potential privacy and safety
concerns were addressed. The amended version of the bill that now sits on the appropriations table reflects the input of both the Maine Coalition to End Domestic Violence and the Maine Coalition Against
Sexual Assault.
We have evidence that this approach works, with effective pilot programs in Aroostook, Penobscot, and Somerset Counties as well as Two Bridges. A small investment of $244,000 as part of this supplemental
budget would take this system statewide, providing an invaluable service to protect the safety and peace of mind to all victims of crime and their loved ones.
Thank you for your thoughtful consideration. I welcome any questions you may have.
Anne Carney

safer and our communities safer.

On LD 2212, An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessaryto the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and
