Members of the Transportation and Appropriations & Financial Affairs Committees. My name is Kris Ladue, and I am a Contract Grant Specialist for the Department of Transportation. I am also the VP of the Transportation Chapter of MSEA-SEIU. I am speaking to you today, on personal time, to address the Pay Gap for State of Maine employees, and how it affects my department, my coworkers, and myself. I am requesting these committees work to use the state government surplus to undo the 2025 personal services budget attrition rates. The increase in the attrition rates took away $68 million from accounts that ought to be used for paying state workers fair wages ($56 million from the General Fund, $12.3 million from the highway budget).
I work for Contract Procurement office that processes the contracts for all programs under DOT. This includes Bridge (which is my program), Multi-Modal, Highway, Maintenance and Operations, Freight and Passenger Services, Project Development, and Planning. Due to the many programs, we have under the CPO umbrella, the workload is heavy, and to stay afloat, we need a complete team to address the needs of DOT.
When I first started three years ago, we were down multiple people, and the workload was intense. My coworkers were balancing not only their own tasks, but the tasks of the vacancies as well. This workload resulted in the implementation of overtime, capped at five hours a week, for straight or comp time. This led to stress, exhaustion, and burnout for myself and my team. Nevertheless, we carried on, and I am proud to say that my crew are the hardest and most resourceful coworkers I ever had the privilege to work with, which dispel the stereotype of state workers. In fact, these perceptions are the exact opposite state employees' realities, since we all are understaffed, overworked, and underpaid.
One of the largest struggles for my department is hiring and retention. Although we now receive a steady number of applicants now due to the current job market, this was not always the case. I believe this was due to the low pay rates at the starting steps of our classification. When we hired new folks, a few that left us within a couple of years. Another struggle is retirement. In the last three years, we lost 6 people in a team that is fully staffed with 10 individuals. It is a process to get new people in the door for the long term, and it is a waste of time and resources to train someone that is gone within the year.
I ask the legislative body today to consider the experience of the state worker in today's world. We are, first and foremost, civil servants, and we deserve to be compensated for our labor at a just rate. With our health insurances premiums rising and inflation, we will be working just to struggle and make ends meet, and I don't believe that is fair nor a sustainable model for the State. I see my coworkers leaving all the time for the private sector, and I honestly do not blame them. My hope is that this legislature will finally address the pay gap so the State can retain its talent, thus offering a good work/life balance and a happy and effect workforce. We

are exhausted, we are undercompensated, and we are struggling, but we show up for the people of the great state of Maine. We just ask for fairness and to reap the fruits of our labor.
Thank you for your time and I'd be happy to answer any questions.
Kris Ladue

10061422:
Testimony of Krystal Williams On Behalf of Alpha Legal Foundation
Senator, Representative, and distinguished members of the Committee:
My name is Krystal Williams. I live in Portland, and I am an attorney, law firm owner, and Katahdin Counsel member, having provided more than 50 hours of documented pro bono representation to indigent Mainers last year. I am also the founder of Alpha Legal Foundation, and I submit this testimony on its behalf.
I respectfully urge you to include $3 million in the FY 2026-27 Supplemental Budget, in addition to the $1.3 million baseline for the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund, to sustain civil legal aid in the second year of the biennium.
Across Maine, a growing number of individuals are navigating the civil court system without representation. In response to what we were seeing on the ground, Alpha Legal Foundation launched a legal access navigator Program in 2025. Through this initiative, we recruit and train non-lawyers interested in pursuing legal careers. Our navigators provide neutral, accurate education about court processes and assist self-represented litigants in completing court forms correctly. Navigators do not provide legal advice. They help individuals understand procedural requirements, organize documentation, and avoid preventable errors that can delay or derail a case.
This work has given us a clear, real-time view of the justice gap.
We routinely encounter:
� individuals who do not understand notice requirements or filing deadlines,
� individuals with limited literacy attempting to complete protection-from-abuse petitions, and
� moderate-income Mainers who earn too much to qualify for free services but cannot afford private counsel and are overwhelmed by basic family court forms.
In each of these situations, the absence of legal support significantly increases the likelihood of an adverse outcome. Education and form assistance can stabilize the process, but they cannot replace the judgment, advocacy, and strategic counsel that licensed attorneys provide, particularly for complex matters.
Our navigators regularly refer individuals to civil legal aid providers. Those providers are already operating at or beyond capacity. The volume of referrals alone demonstrates that demand for representation substantially exceeds available resources. What we are witnessing is not a lack of effort; it is a lack of sufficient infrastructure.

Civil legal aid is core public infrastructure. It prevents unlawful evictions and foreclosures, stabilizes families during crisis, secures access to health care and income supports, protects survivors of violence, and safeguards the rights of children and vulnerable adults. It reduces downstream costs in emergency shelter, health care, and other publicly funded systems.
Without the additional $3 million investment, providers will be forced to reduce services next year. That will mean fewer attorneys available to represent Mainers facing eviction, loss of benefits, or family instability at a time when federal protections and administrative systems are becoming increasingly complex.
Our on-the-ground experience confirms what the data has long shown: the need is substantial, urgent, and growing. Form assistance can help someone enter the courthouse. Only adequately funded civil legal aid ensures they can meaningfully access justice once they are there.
I respectfully urge you to include the requested $3 million in the Supplemental Budget and sustain this essential investment in Maine's legal infrastructure.
Thank you for your time and your continued commitment to Maine's communities.
Krystal Williams, Esq. Alpha Legal Foundation Portland, Maine

10061603:
Testimony of Luisa S. Deprez, PhD, Professor Emerita of Sociology and Social Policy, University of Southern Maine
LD 2122: An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of
the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027
Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs March 9, 2025
Senator Hamper, Representative Rotundo, and members of the Committee Appropriations and Financial Affairs
My name is Luisa S. Deprez. I am Professor Emerita of Sociology and Social Policy at the University of Southern Maine and a member of the Maine chapter of the national Scholars Strategy Network, which brings together scholars across the country to address public challenges and their policy implications.
My work on issues of poverty, social policy, and public assistance and safety net programs in Maine is well-know and long-standing, extending over the past 50 years.
I am here to testify in support of LD 2122 which intends to mitigate the devastating loss of SNAP and Medicaid benefits for thousands of Mainers due to the punishing federal cut-backs. I am grateful to Representative Gattine and his co-sponsors for bringing this legislation forward. It is critically needed.
By 2034, Maine is expected to lose $3.9 billion in total Medicaid and SNAP funding.
Thirty-four thousand (34,000) Mainers are expected to lose Medicaid benefits, and 101,000 households are expected to lose SNAP benefits. These are lifelines for Maine families -- not only for immediate health and food security, but for economic stability across our communities.
These projections come from Visualizing H.R. 1 Cuts Data Dashboard, the recently launched Maine Children's Alliance's (MCA) response to the passage of H.R. 1, aka President Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill Act". Enacted by Congress in July 2025, at the insistence of the President, the bill represents a major shift in federal policies supporting poor, low-income, and working families as it aims to reduce public program enrollment and expenditures. The overall well-being of households is not their concern.
The impact of the cuts will reach deep into Maine: the 53,999 households that rely on both Medicaid and SNAP will be hit hardest. Per capita funding losses will be highest in the rural counties of Washington, Somerset, and Franklin.
You, the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee, and the Maine Legislature, has its work cut out for it as takes up LD 2212: An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027.

The challenge will be to lessen, if not prevent, the negative impacts of H.R.1 on Maine households. Maine Children's Alliance's new interactive resource will help lawmakers to ascertain what is at stake for Maine's children, families, and communities if proposed changes to Medicaid and SNAP proceed without state mitigation. It also shows impact by legislative district so each legislator, each of you, can clearly see the number of households in their/your home district are at risk of losing SNAP benefits and Medicaid coverage as well as expose per capita cuts by county.
While some may assume that H.R.1 is designed to only target the 11% of poor and low-income households in Maine who are allegedly, but wrongly, accused of being solely "dependent" on safety net programs. It does not. It will though further exacerbate the already precarious position that too many Mainers find themselves confronting.
At present, approximately 29% of working families in Maine are below the ALICE (Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed) threshold. These are households with incomes above the Federal Poverty Line but not enough above to afford basic expenses - housing, child care, food, transportation, health care, and technology - in the county in which they live. Households are already forced to make impossible choices -- like deciding whether to pay for utilities or a car repair, whether to buy food or fill a prescription.
Members of these households work in positions that keep our economy functioning smoothly: child care providers, food service workers, cashiers, personal care aides, delivery drivers, nurses' aides, health care counselors, teachers. They represent all demographic groups and their stories capture the systemic and structural barriers, and failures, to financial stability as well as the struggles and resilience of families experiencing financial hardship.
All told, the federal cuts will further stress the already precarious lives for an estimated 40% of households in Maine who are below the ALICE Threshold. And the impact with resonate upward into the middle-class and beyond. No one in the state with be spared; the impacts will ripple not only through families and communities but through the economy of the state.
The implications of H.R.1 funding cutbacks and program eligibility changes cannot be ignored; the impact on Maine households, on Maine, will be too great. By 2034, Maine's loss of Medicaid and SNAP funding is estimated to result in a corresponding 444% increase in the SNAP share of the state budget.
A recent article in the Portland Press Herald shows that the ramifications of H.R.1, coupled with rising prices in just about every arena, are not going unheard. Issues of "affordability" have moved "into the heart of lawmaking". "Shifting federal policy and economic uncertainty are `making it harder for families to get ahead'" says Senate President Mattie Daughtry (DBrunswick). My name is Luisa S. Deprez. Dear Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and Honorable Members of the Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs:
MACDL supports LD 2212 Sections T-18 and T-19 and states as follows.
The Maine Civil Liberties Union (MCLU) filed suit in Robbins v. State of Maine on March 1, 2022. At that time the Maine Commission on Indigent Legal Services (MCILS) was the agency providing indigent criminal legal services in Maine. It was doing its best but had failed to implement several longstanding requirements around the supervision and training of appointed attorneys. The courts were--and in many places still are--struggling under a massive backlog of criminal cases arising from the COVID-19 pandemic. The number of appointed attorneys taking cases was going down while the number of pending cases was going up because the $80 hourly rate paid to appointed attorneys at that time was woefully inadequate.

Progress since March of 2022 has been profound. Training and oversight standards have gone into place. Backlogs have been reduced and, most importantly, the number of people in jails without attorneys has been reduced. The funding of an adequate hourly rate of $150 for appointed attorneys is without question the primary reason for this progress.

The Maine Commission on Public Defense Services (MCPDS), the attorneys it employs, and the attorneys it contracts cannot afford to lose this progress. The State of Maine cannot afford to lose this progress. The current $12M budget shortfall is a truly existential threat to this progress.

Sections T-18 and T-19 of LD 2212 authorize the State Controller to transfer $12,322,443 in FY 2026 and $13,026,035 in FY 2027 to MCPDS. It is no exaggeration to say that MCPDS and the progress made in the last few years cannot survive without this funding. A failure to fully fund

MCPDS will mean attorneys representing accused Mainers across the State will be asked to work without pay. An Act Making Supplemental Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years

Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary
February 27, 2026
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary, greetings. My name is Michael Kebede, and I am policy director for the American Civil Liberties Union of Maine, a statewide organization committed to advancing and preserving civil liberties guaranteed by the Maine and U.S. Constitutions.
On behalf of our members, we urge you to include $3 million in the FY 2026-27 supplemental budget to sustain Maine's statewide civil legal aid network.
Civil legal aid plays a vital role in ensuring meaningful access to justice for Mainers who cannot afford legal representation. In most civil cases-- including those involving housing, family stability, and access to basic necessities--there is no right to counsel. As a result, many low-income Mainers must navigate complex legal proceedings on their own, often against parties with substantially greater resources.
Adequate support for civil legal aid is necessary to ensure that access to the courts does not depend on a person's income. Without legal assistance, many individuals are unable to effectively assert their rights or protect their interests in matters that have profound consequences for their lives and families.
The Legislature made an important investment in civil legal aid in the first year of the biennium. We respectfully urge you to sustain that investment by including $3 million in the FY 2026-27 supplemental budget, in addition to the baseline $1.3 million appropriation. Maintaining this funding will help ensure that civil legal aid providers across Maine can continue to offer assistance to individuals who would otherwise face the legal system alone.

Sustained funding for civil legal aid helps preserve fairness in the legal system and supports the principle that justice should be accessible to all Mainers, regardless of financial means. Thank you for your consideration.

The Association currently represents approximately 2,500 attorneys in the State in both public service and private practice. The Association maintains 28 separate sections covering nearly every field of law practiced in Maine, from Administrative Law to Workers' Compensation Law.
Support for $3 Million in Additional Civil Legal Services Funding for FY27 (Z367). The Maine State Bar Association supports continued and sustained state funding for civil legal services in the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund (Z367), which are essential to ensuring equal access to justice and the fair functioning of Maine's courts. The current biennial budget includes ongoing funding for civil legal services in the amount of $1.3 million for FY27 and beyond. Today, however, we ask the Legislature to supplement this baseline amount by $3 million for a total of $4.3 million in FY27. Notably, the biennial budget for FY 2025-26 included a one-time $3M appropriation to civil legal aid, but this funding was not continued in FY27 and was not addressed in the Supplemental Budget. MSBA Comments re LD 2212 February 23, 2026 Page 2
Civil legal aid provides critical value to the state by helping resolve legal problems efficiently, stabilizing families and communities, and reducing downstream costs to courts and public systems. The presence of qualified attorneys on both sides of civil matters improves the quality of legal proceedings, assists courts in reaching accurate and timely decisions, and supports the integrity and effectiveness of Maine's legal system. MSBA also supports Sections T-18 and T-19 (Z112) of the Supplemental Budget authorizing transfers from the Budget Stabilization Fund to the Maine Commission on Public Defense Services in the amount of $12,322,443 for FY26 and $13,026,035 for FY27. As the Legislature is aware, Maine continues to confront significant challenges in ensuring timely access to constitutionally required counsel for indigent legal defendants. Stable and adequate funding for MCPDS remains essential to maintaining a unified and effective indigent defense system. Providing the resources necessary to meet operational, compliance, and technological needs helps ensure that the State can meet its Sixth Amendment obligations and continue progress toward reducing case backlogs.
Adequate compensation for assigned counsel and continued development of public defender capacity are critical to addressing attorney shortages, managing caseload pressures, and ensuring timely access to counsel. We further note that a significant reason for the current budget shortfall - and the need for this proposed transfer to MCPDS -- is the fact that, when the Legislature raised the hourly fee for assigned counsel to $150/hour, it did not further increase the budget appropriation to account for this change. We respectfully encourage the Committees to support $3 million in additional funding for civil legal services in FY27 and to approve Part T of the Supplemental Budget to support essential MCPDS services in FY26 and FY27.

Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee; Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and members of the Judiciary Committee:
Since 1996, Maine Equal Justice has worked to ensure that people in all sixteen counties have access to the legal help they need to meet basic needs such as staying housed, keeping the heat on, accessing health care, and securing income support. We do this through direct legal representation, policy advocacy to address root causes of poverty, and education and outreach throughout the state.
Maine Equal Justice strongly supports including $3 million in the FY 2026-27 supplemental budget to sustain Maine's civil legal aid network through the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund.
Last year's one-time investment in civil legal aid strengthened our ability, and the capacity of our partners, to respond to growing needs across Maine. Without action this session, that funding will not continue into the second year of the biennium, resulting in reduced access to legal assistance for Maine households facing serious legal challenges. This funding maintains the service capacity already authorized by the Legislature and prevents a significant reduction in services.
Every day, our legal team works with people facing urgent barriers to stability. Legal aid is often the difference between keeping and losing housing, maintaining access to health care, or securing essential income support. Beyond helping people through crises, legal aid can be a turning point that allows individuals and families to move toward long-term stability and economic opportunity.
In 2025, Maine Equal Justice handled 919 individual cases across all sixteen counties, helping individuals and families address issues related to housing, health coverage, employment, education, and income support. Housing and income-related cases represented the largest areas of need, reflecting the economic pressures facing Maine households.
Maine Equal Justice also provides legal assistance to individuals who may not be eligible for services through other legal aid providers. In 2025, we represented 42 immigrants facing eviction and achieved a 93 percent success rate in preventing displacement or securing favorable outcomes, ensuring that access to justice extends to all members of our communities.

Alongside individual representation, Maine Equal Justice engages in systemic advocacy to improve the functioning of public benefit programs and remove barriers that prevent eligible Mainers from accessing support. In 2025, this work included administrative and policy advocacy that improved access to food assistance, health coverage, workforce programs, and energy assistance for tens of thousands of Maine residents.
Maine Equal Justice sustains its work through a combination of public and private funding, including the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund, Interest on Lawyers' Trust Accounts (IOLTA), the Campaign for Justice, foundation grants, and individual donors. The Maine Civil Legal Services Fund provides critical general operating support that is essential to maintaining MEJ's legal services and statewide capacity.
Rising costs of living have significantly increased unmet basic needs across Maine, driving higher demand for civil legal assistance. The ongoing housing crisis and increasing instability in public benefit programs have led to growing numbers of Mainers seeking legal help to maintain housing, secure income supports, and access health coverage.
The one-time funding provided through the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund allowed Maine Equal Justice to sustain expanded staffing capacity in 2025 and respond to this growing demand. Without that funding, we would not have been able to serve hundreds of Maine households who needed legal assistance to maintain basic stability.
If this funding is not sustained in FY 2026-27, Maine Equal Justice will be forced to reduce staffing and limit the number of cases we can take. This will mean fewer Maine households receiving legal assistance and more individuals and families facing housing loss, benefit terminations, and other legal crises without help.
These reductions would affect communities across Maine. In 2025, Maine Equal Justice provided legal assistance to households in all sixteen counties, and reduced capacity would mean fewer constituents able to access legal help when they need it most.
Demand for civil legal assistance continues to grow. Sustaining this funding will allow Maine Equal Justice and our partners to continue serving Maine households and addressing legal problems before they escalate into deeper economic crises.
We respectfully urge the Legislature to include $3 million in the FY 2026-27 supplemental budget to sustain Maine's civil legal aid network and preserve access to justice for Maine households.
Thank you for your consideration.

10061409:
Testimony of Susan Roche, Executive Director of the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project
in Support of Supplemental Budget Funding for Civil Legal Aid
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee; Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and members of the Judiciary Committee.
My name is Susan Roche, and I am the Executive Director of the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project (ILAP). I am submitting this testimony to strongly support the inclusion of $3 million in the FY 2026-27 supplemental budget to sustain Maine's civil legal aid network through the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund (MCLSF). ILAP is one of the seven civil legal aid organizations that receives funding from MCLSF.
ILAP is Maine's only statewide immigration legal services organization. Founded in 1993, ILAP's mission is to advance justice for Maine's immigrants through free immigration legal services, community outreach, and advocacy.
ILAP serves over 5,000 clients each year in all 16 of Maine's counties. We reach communities statewide through legal clinics, education and outreach, virtual legal services, "self-help" materials, statewide advocacy, and partnerships that extend our reach across the state. We provide free, specialized immigration legal representation to individuals and families in Maine with a focus on humanitarian cases and cases involving detention and removal. During the past year our work in detention and removal, and now federal habeas work, has expanded significantly.
Last year's one-time investment in civil legal aid provided ILAP with the ability to expand our capacity to help more immigrants in Maine at a time when draconian federal immigration policies and enhanced detention and enforcement operations have had a devastating impact on immigrants in Maine and significantly increased the complexity of our work.
Having an immigration lawyer can be the difference between having legal status in the U.S. and being deported back to a country where you face persecution and family separation. Statistics show that someone is five times more likely to win their case in immigration court if they have a lawyer. ILAP maintains a success rate of over 95% for cases reaching a final decision.
In this time of heightened immigration enforcement, legal representation is even more critical in an immigration case, as many people are being detained who have pending legal immigration applications, work authorization, and no criminal history. They are quickly transferred out of state, held under horrible conditions in detention facilities, and denied a hearing or coerced

into signing away their right to a hearing. Without rapid legal intervention they are extremely unlikely to get released from jail or to be given the right to proceed with their legal immigration case before getting deported, possibly to a third country where they have no connection or legal status.
Most recently, during "Operation Catch of the Day" ILAP expanded its habeas work and worked in collaboration with partners including the Refugee and Human Rights Clinic at the University of Maine School of Law to develop a rapid emergency response plan. During the four-day operation, ICE detained over 200 immigrants in Maine, and most of them had pending immigration applications and no criminal history. ILAP received requests for help from about 70 individuals, and we filed 17 habeas petitions. Of those cases, most individuals have already been released because of our legal advocacy.
One client from the operation was deaf and spoke an uncommon form of sign language and was unable to communicate with ICE or understand what was happening. Another client was a father whose baby was in the NICU and whose wife was home recovering from surgery after childbirth. Both clients had pending immigration applications, work authorization, and no criminal history. They were both released but would likely have been deported without legal representation.
Although Operation Catch of the Day has ended, enhanced ICE enforcement and raids continue. We have continued the work of our emergency legal response as more individuals have been detained over the past couple of weeks and we are working on plans for a more sustainable project, which will require increased staffing and capacity.
Immigration enforcement has had a chilling effect on communities, as many immigrant families, including those with naturalized US citizens and legal permanent residents, are afraid to leave their homes, send their children to school, go to the doctor, or call the police for help when they are the victim of a crime. The ICE operation has had a ripple effect impacting other areas of civil legal aid as many are now facing eviction, losing their jobs, and much more.
Funding from the MCLSF was critical in helping ILAP increase staffing and capacity to respond to the increased demand for our services resulting from new immigration policies and enforcement. For ILAP, the MCLSF is our only form of recurring government funding. We are ineligible for most federal funding because of the clients we serve. So, we rely upon private donors and funders for most of our support, and that funding is subject to shifting priorities and changing donor interests.
Losing the MCLSF funding could not come at a worse time, when immigrant communities in Maine and throughout the country are the target of a mass deportation and detention campaign, when lawful paths to legal status are being eliminated, and when due process and the rule of law are being eroded. Decreased funding would lead to fewer attorneys on ILAP's staff to represent vulnerable Mainers who are caught up in ICE enforcement and detention.
2

As more immigrants with lawful work authorization are detained, transferred out of state, and deported, this will have a devastating impact on Maine's communities, workforce, and economy. Investing in civil legal aid is an investment in Maine and our communities. I respectfully urge the Legislature to include $3 million in the FY 2026-27 supplemental budget to sustain Maine's civil legal aid network and preserve access to justice for low-income Mainers. Thank you for your consideration.
3

So, we rely upon private donors and funders for most of our support, and that funding is subject to shifting priorities and changing donor interests.
Losing the MCLSF funding could not come at a worse time, when immigrant communities in Maine and throughout the country are the target of a mass deportation and detention campaign, when lawful paths to legal status are being eliminated, and when due process and the rule of law are being eroded. Decreased funding would lead to fewer attorneys on ILAP's staff to represent vulnerable Mainers who are caught up in ICE enforcement and detention.
As more immigrants with lawful work authorization are detained, transferred out of state, and deported, this will have a devastating impact on Maine's communities, workforce, and economy. Investing in civil legal aid is an investment in Maine and our communities.
I respectfully urge the Legislature to include $3 million in the FY 2026-27 supplemental budget to sustain Maine's civil legal aid network and preserve access to justice for low-income Mainers.
Thank you for your consideration.

Testimony of Tom Fritzsche on behalf of Pine Tree Legal Assistance before the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary and the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee
In Support of Amending LD 2212 to Prevent Reductions in Legal Services to People with Low Incomes and to Protect Services for Survivors of Sexual Assault and Domestic Violence
February 27, 2026
Good afternoon, Senators Rotundo and Carney, Representatives Gattine and Kuhn, and esteemed members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary.
My name is Tom Fritzsche, and I am the Executive Director of Pine Tree Legal Assistance. Pine Tree Legal Assistance strongly supports the amendment of LD 2212 to prevent a reduction of $3 million in the critical funding to the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund (MCLSF) that allows Pine Tree Legal Assistance and six other non-profit service organizations to provide access to justice to low-income Mainers. Pine Tree Legal Assistance further supports making previously appropriated funds to support legal and advocacy services provided to survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault ongoing.
Pine Tree Legal Assistance opened its doors in the summer of 1967 and has six offices throughout the state, in Presque Isle, Machias, Bangor, Augusta, Lewiston and Portland. Our staff handle cases in all 16 counties, in all 26 district courts, and in the tribal courts of the Passamaquoddy Tribe and Penobscot Nation. We are Maine's largest non-profit provider of legal services, and for many Mainers needing legal help for housing stability, protection from abuse or harassment, consumer rights, and many other basic needs, Pine Tree is their first and last resort. We represent low-income Mainers statewide with no fees to our clients.
If the $3 million in one-time funding appropriated in 2025 expires in June 2026, as it is currently on track to do, the seven service providers are likely to serve a total of at least 5,000 fewer clients next year than we did last year. The impact will last beyond 2026 and 2027; the outreach and referral networks, trained attorney and paralegal staff, and other infrastructure are harder to recreate once they go away than they are to sustain. More importantly, families with children will be evicted without counsel and will face greater, and longer-lasting, disruption to the stability of their housing, education, and access to employment and medical care. Survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault who do not have legal representation will be more likely to

be stuck in abusive relationships. Low-income consumers and homeowners will be more likely to lose their homes and funds and will face future poverty that could have been prevented by our state's laws, if all had equal access to justice. The consequences of unequal access to justice will stay with people and communities for years to come.
To illustrate what is possible with funding to the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund and other sources of support, I include below data regarding Pine Tree Legal Assistance's Services and Impact during 2025. Additional details are available in our full report to the Maine Civil Legal Services Fund Commission, available on the website of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary.
Just in 2025, Pine Tree Legal Assistance worked on a total of 7,858 cases. Pine Tree reached more than 27,000 people in 2025 through our direct legal services and outreach. This included 18,157 people served through individual cases, including 6,311 children, and 9,013 people served through community education activities including consultations, meetings, presentations, and trainings.
MCLSF funding is crucial for the maintenance and development of website resources and selfhelp tools. Pine Tree maintains three websites: ptla.org, kidslegal.org, and statesidelegal.org. All three websites are freely available to any individual and remain an important way of increasing access to the justice system, especially for unrepresented individuals. Pine Tree's websites are nationally recognized for their accessibility and successful provision of tools for unrepresented people to navigate the legal system when they need to do so. In 2025, Pine Tree's websites were utilized by 2,047,482 unique users in 2025, accessing Pine Tree's websites for a total of 2,691,154 page views. These statistics include users who accessed our chatbot in 2025. Ptla.org alone recorded 1,773,645 users and 2,170,277 page views.
The following data highlights some of Pine Tree's most significant outcomes. In 2025, Pine Tree's advocacy:
� Resulted in $4,176,970 in income, savings, and benefits to our clients. � Prevented homelessness for 2,060 households by preventing or delaying an eviction. � Preserved housing subsidies for eligible tenant families worth more than $225,000
annually. � Secured more than 368 new or extended protection orders for victims of domestic
violence, sexual assault, stalking, and dating violence.
The data collected on outcomes provides only a glimpse into the impact of Pine Tree's advocacy. Further, despite our best efforts, we are not able to serve all of the people who contact us looking for legal services. In 2025, Pine Tree Legal Assistance recorded 10,282 requests for legal help. Just under 65% of the requests for assistance resulted in a new case. The remaining 36% were addressed with general legal information and/or referrals to other resources. It would be an enormous setback to see the latter number increase in the coming year if MCSLF funding drops off after June 30.

One of the areas of our work at greatest risk due to funding reductions is our focus on services in rural Maine. For example, Aroostook and Washington counties make up one-third of the entire state of Maine but have fewer than 100 working attorneys - less than 3 percent of all working attorneys in Maine. While these counties may have low population densities, their need for legal assistance remains high. A 2022 national survey conducted by the Legal Services Corporation found that 77 percent of low-income rural households experienced at least one civil legal problem in the previous year. Despite the great need for legal aid in Maine's rural regions, recruiting and retaining attorneys in these remote areas has proven challenging. Pine Tree Legal Assistance has invested MCLSF resources into staffing our Machias and Presque Isle offices with newer attorneys, with positive early returns that will be impossible to sustain without ongoing MCLSF support.
Pine Tree Legal Assistance also supports making funding previously appropriated to support the work of advocates and staff at Maine's sexual assault support centers and children's advocacy centers ongoing, to help those staff continue their badly needed work, which also often makes legal services to those clients that PTLA staff provide more effective. Pine Tree Legal Assistance further supports making funding previously appropriated to support services partially funded by the federal Victims of Crime Act, some of which is one-time and will expire in 2027, ongoing, in order to ensure that legal and advocacy services are sustained well into the future.
Thank you for your time and for your dedication to the people of Maine. Please do not hesitate to contact me with any questions.
